Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a parametric statistical model, let $p\ge1$, and let
$X:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be a measurable random vector with
$\mathbb E_\theta\|X\|_2^2<\infty$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. Write
$\mu_\theta=\mathbb E_\theta X$ and
$\Sigma_\theta=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X)$ as in
[[def-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]]. The map
$\psi(\theta)=\Sigma_\theta$ is the covariance-matrix estimand on this model
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

For each $\theta$, list the real eigenvalues of $\Sigma_\theta$ in
nonincreasing order and counting multiplicity. The **covariance-PCA
decomposition** is the list of eigenspaces of $\Sigma_\theta$, ordered by
their distinct eigenvalues from largest to smallest. Equivalently, for each
distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$, its component subspace is
$\ker(\Sigma_\theta-\lambda I)$. The top eigenspace is the leading principal
subspace; when its eigenvalue is simple it is a line, and either unit
representative has the same sign-free direction.
The well-definedness result
[[lem-finite-second-moment-covariance-matrix-is-well-defined]] ensures these
covariance matrices are finite, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The
real spectral theorem
[[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] ensures their
eigenspaces span $\mathbb R^p$.

If every coordinate variance $(\Sigma_\theta)_{jj}$ is positive, put
$D_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(\Sigma_\theta)_{11}},\ldots,
\sqrt{(\Sigma_\theta)_{pp}})$ and standardize the centered vector as
$Z_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}(X-\mu_\theta)$. Its covariance is the correlation
matrix
$R_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}\Sigma_\theta D_\theta^{-1}$. **Correlation-PCA** is
the ordered eigenspace decomposition of $R_\theta$. Thus both population
conventions center first; correlation-PCA additionally divides each
coordinate by its positive population standard deviation.

For an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, **sample covariance-PCA** uses the
eigenspaces of the sample-centered covariance
$\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast=n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T}$
from [[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]], where
$\bar X=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$. Sample correlation-PCA standardizes by the
positive sample standard deviations when all sample coordinate variances are
positive. The divisor convention here is $n$, not $n-1$. The sample
covariance matrix is a statistic, and it is an estimator of the covariance
target in its sample experiment, as proved in
[[lem-pca-sample-covariance-is-a-measurable-estimator]].

This definition specifies mathematical matrices under an assumed law. The
scientific model contract distinguishes that assumption from evidence that an
empirical law is adequate; PCA itself makes no such adequacy claim
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be self-adjoint on an $n$-dimensional real inner product space,
and list its eigenvalues in weakly decreasing order:

$$\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n.$$

Then for every $1\le k\le n$,

$$\lambda_k=\min_{\dim W=n-k+1}\ \max_{0\ne v\in W} R_T(v)=\max_{\dim U=k}\ \min_{0\ne v\in U} R_T(v).$$

derivations.claim: Put $Y=X-\mu_\theta$. Finite second moments make every coordinate in the finite sums below integrable. Expanding the centered scalar square and using [F4] gives $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(a^{\mathsf T}X) =\mathbb E_\theta[(a^{\mathsf T}Y)^2] =\sum_{j,k}a_ja_k\mathbb E_\theta[Y_jY_k] =a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\theta a$ by [F2] and [F3].

By [F5], write $a=\sum_{j=1}^pc_je_j$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\Sigma_\theta$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_p$ and $\sum_jc_j^2=1$. Then $a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\theta a=\sum_j\lambda_jc_j^2\le\lambda_1\sum_jc_j^2 =\lambda_1$. The difference is $\lambda_1-a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\theta a =\sum_j(\lambda_1-\lambda_j)c_j^2$, a sum of nonnegative terms, so equality holds exactly when $c_j=0$ for every $\lambda_j<\lambda_1$. This is exactly the unit sphere in the leading eigenspace. Step 1.1 identifies this Rayleigh quotient with projected variance, proving the covariance-PCA assertion.

If all coordinate variances are positive, [F1] defines $Z_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}(X-\mu_\theta)$ with covariance $R_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}\Sigma_\theta D_\theta^{-1}$. The hypotheses of steps 1.1--2.1 hold with $Z_\theta$ and $R_\theta$ in place of $X$ and $\Sigma_\theta$, so the leading correlation-PCA eigenspace maximizes the variance of unit linear scores of $Z_\theta$.

Fix $p\ge1$ and a Borel probability law $P$ on $\mathbb R^p$ with
$\mathbb E_P\|X\|_2^4<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance matrix $\Sigma$.
For each $n\ge1$, let $X_{n,1},\ldots,X_{n,n}$ be iid with law $P$; the
probability space may depend on $n$. Put
$$ \bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i},\qquad \widehat\Sigma_n^\ast:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_{n,i}-\bar X_n)(X_{n,i}-\bar X_n)^{\mathsf T}, $$
the sample-centered covariance with divisor $n$ from
[[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]]. For a matrix $B$, define
$\|B\|_F:=(\sum_{j,k=1}^pB_{jk}^2)^{1/2}$. Then
$$
\|\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast-\Sigma\|_F=O_P(n^{-1/2}),
$$
meaning $\sqrt n\|\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast-\Sigma\|_F=O_P(1)$ in the
bounded-in-probability sense of
[[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]]. No Gaussian assumption is needed.

Let $p\ge2$, let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, and order its
eigenvalues as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_p(A)$. Suppose its leading
eigenvalue is simple, with gap
$$
g:=\lambda_1(A)-\lambda_2(A)>0,
$$
and let $v$ be a unit leading eigenvector. Let $E\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be
symmetric, put $\epsilon:=\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, and assume
$0\le\epsilon<g/2$. If $\widetilde v$ is any unit leading eigenvector of
$A+E$, then the leading eigenvalue of $A+E$ is simple and
$$ |\lambda_1(A+E)-\lambda_1(A)|\le\epsilon,\qquad \sin\angle(v,\widetilde v):=\sqrt{1-(v^{\mathsf T}\widetilde v)^2}\le\frac{\epsilon}{g-\epsilon}. $$
The bound concerns the line spanned by the eigenvector, so it is unchanged by
either sign choice. It is a local eigengap bound; it does not assert a
dimension-free Davis--Kahan theorem or a finite-sample inference procedure.

Let $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a family of Borel probability laws on
$\mathbb R^p$ with $\mathbb E_\theta\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. For each $n\ge1$,
observe an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with common law $P_\theta$ and sample
law $P_\theta^{\otimes n}$ on the Borel data space $(\mathbb R^p)^n$. Put
$\Sigma_\theta=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X)$ and let
$\psi(\theta)=\Sigma_\theta$ be the covariance-matrix estimand with target
the Borel space $\mathbb S^p$ of real symmetric $p\times p$ matrices. The
sample-centered covariance map
$$ T_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i, $$
is a statistic with target the Borel space $\mathbb S^p$, and hence is an
estimator of $\psi$ in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. This
statement asserts measurability and target type only; it asserts no
unbiasedness or consistency.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

eigenvalues as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_p(A)$. Suppose its leading
eigenvalue is simple, with gap
$$
g:=\lambda_1(A)-\lambda_2(A)>0,
$$
and let $v$ be a unit leading eigenvector. Let $E\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be

$$ |\lambda_1(A+E)-\lambda_1(A)|\le\epsilon,\qquad \sin\angle(v,\widetilde v):=\sqrt{1-(v^{\mathsf T}\widetilde v)^2}\le\frac{\epsilon}{g-\epsilon}. $$

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a parametric statistical model, let $p\ge1$, and let
$X:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be a measurable random vector with
$\mathbb E_\theta\|X\|_2^2<\infty$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. Write
$\mu_\theta=\mathbb E_\theta X$ and
$\Sigma_\theta=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X)$ as in
[[def-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]]. The map
$\psi(\theta)=\Sigma_\theta$ is the covariance-matrix estimand on this model
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

For each $\theta$, list the real eigenvalues of $\Sigma_\theta$ in
nonincreasing order and counting multiplicity. The **covariance-PCA
decomposition** is the list of eigenspaces of $\Sigma_\theta$, ordered by
their distinct eigenvalues from largest to smallest. Equivalently, for each
distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$, its component subspace is
$\ker(\Sigma_\theta-\lambda I)$. The top eigenspace is the leading principal
subspace; when its eigenvalue is simple it is a line, and either unit
representative has the same sign-free direction.
The well-definedness result
[[lem-finite-second-moment-covariance-matrix-is-well-defined]] ensures these
covariance matrices are finite, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The
real spectral theorem
[[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] ensures their
eigenspaces span $\mathbb R^p$.

If every coordinate variance $(\Sigma_\theta)_{jj}$ is positive, put
$D_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(\Sigma_\theta)_{11}},\ldots,
\sqrt{(\Sigma_\theta)_{pp}})$ and standardize the centered vector as
$Z_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}(X-\mu_\theta)$. Its covariance is the correlation
matrix
$R_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}\Sigma_\theta D_\theta^{-1}$. **Correlation-PCA** is
the ordered eigenspace decomposition of $R_\theta$. Thus both population
conventions center first; correlation-PCA additionally divides each
coordinate by its positive population standard deviation.

For an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, **sample covariance-PCA** uses the
eigenspaces of the sample-centered covariance
$\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast=n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T}$
from [[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]], where
$\bar X=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$. Sample correlation-PCA standardizes by the
positive sample standard deviations when all sample coordinate variances are
positive. The divisor convention here is $n$, not $n-1$. The sample
covariance matrix is a statistic, and it is an estimator of the covariance
target in its sample experiment, as proved in
[[lem-pca-sample-covariance-is-a-measurable-estimator]].

This definition specifies mathematical matrices under an assumed law. The
scientific model contract distinguishes that assumption from evidence that an
empirical law is adequate; PCA itself makes no such adequacy claim
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Fix a parameter $\theta$ in the model of
[[def-covariance-and-correlation-principal-component-analysis]], and let
$X$ have finite second moment and covariance matrix $\Sigma_\theta$. For
every unit vector $a\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$ \operatorname{Var}_\theta(a^{\mathsf T}X)=a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\theta a. $$

Let $n,p\ge1$ and $q\ge0$ be finite integers. A **finite-dimensional linear mixed model** on one probability space consists of fixed matrices $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and $Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}$, a fixed parameter $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$, and square-integrable random vectors $b\in\mathbb R^q$ and $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R^n$ such that
$$
Y=X\beta+Zb+\varepsilon,\qquad \mathbb E b=0,\qquad \mathbb E\varepsilon=0,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(b)=G,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)=R,
$$
where $b$ and $\varepsilon$ are independent random elements. Here $G$ and $R$ are the resulting symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrices. The fixed-design convention for $X$ and the first-moment regression model is that of [[def-fixed-design-linear-regression-model]]. The explicit scientific record of units, quantities, observation mechanism, and adequacy assumptions is required by [[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]].

For longitudinal data, let $j$ index subjects and let $i\in S_j$ index the visits scheduled for subject $j$. A row of $Y$, $X$, and $Z$ corresponds to one observed subject–visit pair $(j,i)$; the time $t_{ji}$ is measured from a stated origin. Blocks of $b$ may represent subject-specific latent effects, while $R$ records the residual covariance across observed rows. If a visit pattern is fixed or conditioned on, the corresponding rows are selected from the scheduled vectors and matrices. If the pattern is random, its observation mechanism is specified separately; the displayed model does not assert that this mechanism is independent of the full outcomes or ignorable for likelihood inference.

The definition imposes no Gaussianity, no identical visit schedule, and no claim that a scientific application satisfies the proposed mean or covariance structure.

For the moment model $Y=X\beta+Zb+\varepsilon$ of [[def-linear-mixed-model]], the marginal covariance is
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=V:=ZGZ^T+R.
$$
This identity uses only the stated means, covariances, and independence; it does not require Gaussianity.

Let $m=\sum_j|S_j|$ and let $Y^*\in\mathbb R^m$ be the complete scheduled response vector for subjects $j$ and visits $i$. Let the declared observed covariates take values in a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. The finite set of observation patterns is $\mathcal R=\{0,1\}^m$; $r_{ji}=1$ means visit $(j,i)$ is observed. A missingness mechanism is a function $g:\mathcal R\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ such that, for every $(y^*,x)$, $\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}g(r\mid y^*,x)=1$, and, for each fixed $r$, $(y^*,x)\mapsto g(r\mid y^*,x)$ is measurable for $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal A$. Thus $g(\cdot\mid y^*,x)$ is a probability mass function on $\mathcal R$, and its dependence on the full data state is the finite-output kernel specified by the observation-mechanism field in [[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]], which requires a probability measure at each state and measurable state dependence. For a pattern $r$, write $Y_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$ for the subvector of $Y^*$ at coordinates with $r_{ji}=1$.

The mechanism is **missing completely at random (MCAR)** if, for each pattern $r$, $g(r\mid y^*,x)$ does not depend on $y^*$. It is **missing at random (MAR)** if, for each $r$, it depends on the full response vector only through $Y_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$ and $x$. It is **missing not at random (MNAR)** relative to this partition if the MAR condition fails for at least one pattern on the declared support. **Monotone dropout** means that, within each subject, observed visits form an initial segment of the scheduled visits, possibly empty or complete.

These are properties of the declared observation kernel. A mixed-model mean or covariance equation does not specify the kernel or imply MCAR, MAR, or MNAR.

Let
$$
\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})
$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). When the model is
parametric, write $\mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). A **scientific statistical model
contract** is an explicit record of the following fields for a specified
analysis.

1. **Observation space and record.** Give $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and say
   which values form one recorded data object. A response and each predictor
   used as a function of the data must be a specified measurable map from this
   space to a named measurable target. This is the map convention for a
   statistic in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; it does not make a predictor
   causal or the response law correct.

2. **Scientific, sampling, assignment, and analysis units.** Name the
   biological or physical unit about which the scientific question is asked,
   the sample unit selected for observation when sampling occurs, the
   assignment unit receiving a randomized treatment when randomization occurs,
   and the analysis unit represented in each data record. These roles may
   differ. A technical replicate is a repeated reading or assay of the same
   specimen; a biological replicate is a distinct biological unit. Neither
   term asserts independence. State whether enrollment is a probability
   sample or a specified convenience/design cohort.

3. **Indices and time.** Give every unit, treatment, visit, and repeated
   measurement index, the object each index identifies, and the time origin.
   In particular, do not identify a participant index with a visit or assay
   index merely because all are written as rows in a data array.

4. **Quantity status.** Mark each model quantity as **fixed** (held
   nonrandom under the declared law), **random** (a measurable random element
   with its law specified, using [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]
   and [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]), **observed** (recorded
   in the data object), or **latent** (part of a fuller model state but not
   recorded). A latent quantity must separately be declared fixed or random.
   If inference conditions on a design value or event, name it and state the
   conditional law being used.

5. **Target and estimand.** Name the target population of units, settings,
   and time period, and distinguish it from the enrolled or observed sample.
   Specify the target as a function $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T$ when it is an
   estimand in the parametric model, as in
   [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]. The contract alone does not show
   that the target is identifiable. Identifiability means that equality of
   sampling laws forces equality of target values
   ([[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]).

6. **Observation mechanism.** State how a fuller scientific state becomes
   the recorded data. A deterministic mechanism is a specified measurable map
   $O:(\mathcal W,\mathcal G)\to(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. A stochastic
   mechanism is specified by $K:\mathcal W\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ such that,
   for each $w$, $A\mapsto K(w,A)$ is a probability measure and, for each
   $A\in\mathcal A$, $w\mapsto K(w,A)$ is measurable. These clauses define the
   mechanism supplied by the contract; they do not assert that a conditional
   version exists for an arbitrary joint law.

7. **Support and law.** State the sampling law $P_\theta$ on
   $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. For an asserted support set, give a measurable
   $S_\theta\subseteq\mathcal X$ with $P_\theta(S_\theta)=1$. If “support”
   instead means topological support, name the topology and the conditions
   under which that convention is being used. If densities are used, name the
   dominating measure and state whether their positive sets agree across
   parameter values. For a randomized design, also state its assignment law;
   if inference averages over assignments, give the resulting joint law.

8. **Conditioning convention.** Say whether inference uses the joint law,
   averaging over the declared randomization, or a specified conditional law
   given the realized design. A conditional law at an event of probability
   zero must be supplied as a specified version with its existence
   hypotheses; it is not defined by an ordinary probability ratio.

9. **Adequacy assumptions.** List each scientific adequacy assumption and
   classify it as **design-controlled** (imposed by protocol and checked
   against implementation records), **empirically assessable** (data or
   validation measurements can challenge it, without proving it true), or
   **substantively untestable** from the declared observed-data law (external
   domain evidence or additional assumptions are needed). Split an assumption
   that has different parts into separate entries and justify each label.

These are bookkeeping and interpretation requirements. They do not assert that
an empirical law equals a proposed model, that a design was implemented as
specified, that calibration is valid, or that any scientific or physical
application is adequate. No independence, exchangeability, missingness,
causal-identification, or common-support assumption follows from the indexing
or the classification labels. This definition uses no axiom of choice.

derivations.claim: The signs are centered, square-integrable, and independent; $b$ is independent of $\varepsilon$. Thus this is a moment-only random-intercept mixed model with $G=[1]$ and $R=I_2$. By [F2], its complete-response covariance is $\operatorname{Cov}\begin{pmatrix}Y_1\\Y_2\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}+I_2 =\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.$

Let the pattern space be $\mathcal R=\{0,1\}^2$ with its power-set $\sigma$-algebra, and define the full observation-pattern map $O(y_1,y_2)=(1,\mathbf 1\{y_2=2\})$. It is Borel measurable because its first coordinate is constant and its second is the indicator of a Borel set. The induced kernel $K(y,A)=\mathbf 1\{O(y)\in A\}$ is the point mass at $O(y)$ for each $y$; for every $A\subseteq\mathcal R$, $y\mapsto K(y,A)$ is measurable as the indicator of the Borel set $O^{-1}(A)$. Thus [F4] applies. Each sign triple has probability $1/8$. The two supported states $(1,-1,-1)$ and $(1,-1,1)$ both give observed first-visit value $Y_1=0$, but their second-visit values are $Y_2=0$ and $Y_2=2$, respectively; their patterns are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

For the missing-visit pattern $r=(1,0)$, the mechanism probability is $1$ at $(Y_1,Y_2)=(0,0)$ and $0$ at $(0,2)$. These supported full-data points have the same observed coordinates $Y_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)=Y_1=0$, so this pattern probability cannot depend only on the observed data for $r$. By [F3], the mechanism is not MAR, despite the correct random-intercept covariance in step 1.1.

The **Gaussian branch** of [[def-linear-mixed-model]] adds the following assumption: under the Axiom of Choice, the concatenated vector
$$
W=\begin{pmatrix}b\\ \varepsilon\end{pmatrix}
$$
has the multivariate-normal law $N_{q+n}(0,\operatorname{diag}(G,R))$ of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Thus the full latent-effect and residual vector is jointly Gaussian. This is an additional branch; the moment-only definition and the covariance identity do not assume Gaussianity.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $U=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and let
$y:U\to\mathbb R$ be a fixed function. The pair $(U,y)$ is a **finite
population**; its **total** and **mean** are
$$T(y):=\sum_{i\in U}y_i,\qquad \bar y_U:=T(y)/N.$$

A **sampling design** on $U$ is a nonempty finite set
$\mathcal S_d\subseteq\mathcal P(U)$ and a function
$p_d:\mathcal S_d\to(0,1]$ with $\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_d}p_d(s)=1$.
Here $\mathcal S_d$ is the support of the design law: zero-weight subsets are
omitted. Thus $(\mathcal S_d,p_d)$ is a finite probability space in the sense
of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $A\subseteq\mathcal S_d$
and $g:\mathcal S_d\to\mathbb R$, put
$$P_d(A):=\sum_{s\in A}p_d(s),\qquad E_d[g]:=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_d}p_d(s)g(s).$$
The random sample is the subset $S\in\mathcal S_d$; probability and
expectation here average over the design while holding every $y_i$ fixed.

For $i,j\in U$, define the **inclusion indicator**
$$I_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&i\in s,\\0,&i\notin s,\end{cases}$$
the **first-order inclusion probability**
$$\pi_i:=P_d(\{s\in\mathcal S_d:i\in s\}),$$
and the **second-order inclusion probability**
$$\pi_{ij}:=P_d(\{s\in\mathcal S_d:i,j\in s\}).$$
In particular, $\pi_{ii}=\pi_i$.

The observed record includes the selected unit labels and their values. For a
common record space set
$$\mathcal X_d:=\{(s,z):s\in\mathcal S_d,\ z:s\to\mathbb R\},\qquad \mathcal A_d:=\mathcal P(\mathcal X_d),$$
and for each $y\in\mathbb R^U$ define
$$O_y(s):=(s,y|_s),\qquad P_y^d(B):=\sum_{\substack{s\in\mathcal S_d\\O_y(s)\in B}}p_d(s)\quad(B\in\mathcal A_d).$$
For a real-valued statistic $h$ on $\mathcal X_d$, write
$$E_y^d[h]:=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_d}p_d(s)h(O_y(s))=E_d[h\circ O_y];$$
this is expectation under the induced observed-data law.
The local well-definedness result
[[lem-finite-population-design-law-is-a-probability-measure]] shows that each
$P_y^d$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X_d,\mathcal A_d)$. Hence
$$\mathsf E_d:=((\mathcal X_d,\mathcal A_d),\mathbb R^U,(P_y^d)_{y\in\mathbb R^U})$$
is a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), with parametric
model $\mathsf P_d(y)=P_y^d$ ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). The total
$y\mapsto T(y)$ and mean $y\mapsto\bar y_U$ are estimands
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

This is design probability: the $y_i$ are fixed and only $S$ is random. A
superpopulation model instead assigns a probability law to the values $y_i$;
that additional law is separate from $p_d$. The finite-population target and
the sampling unit must be recorded in the scientific model contract
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]). In fixed-design regression,
the matrix $X$ is held fixed and has no selection law; that convention alone
does not specify a sampling design on $U$
([[def-fixed-design-linear-regression-model]]).

Let $(U,y)$ be a finite population and let $p_d$ be a sampling design as in
[[def-finite-population-and-sampling-design]]. Suppose $\pi_i>0$ for every
$i\in U$. Give the real target space its Borel sigma-algebra. For an observed
record $(s,z)\in\mathcal X_d$, define
$$\widehat T_{HT}(s,z):=\sum_{i\in s}\frac{z_i}{\pi_i},\qquad \widehat{\bar y}_{HT}(s,z):=\frac{\widehat T_{HT}(s,z)}{N}.$$
Under the induced observed-data law $P_y^d$, these are estimators of the
finite-population total and mean, respectively, and
$$E_y^d[\widehat T_{HT}]=T(y),\qquad E_y^d[\widehat{\bar y}_{HT}]=\bar y_U.$$

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

citations.quote:
Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $U=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and let
$y:U\to\mathbb R$ be a fixed function. The pair $(U,y)$ is a **finite
population**; its **total** and **mean** are
$$T(y):=\sum_{i\in U}y_i,\qquad \bar y_U:=T(y)/N.$$

A **sampling design** on $U$ is a nonempty finite set
$\mathcal S_d\subseteq\mathcal P(U)$ and a function
$p_d:\mathcal S_d\to(0,1]$ with $\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_d}p_d(s)=1$.
Here $\mathcal S_d$ is the support of the design law: zero-weight subsets are
omitted. Thus $(\mathcal S_d,p_d)$ is a finite probability space in the sense
of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $A\subseteq\mathcal S_d$
and $g:\mathcal S_d\to\mathbb R$, put
$$P_d(A):=\sum_{s\in A}p_d(s),\qquad E_d[g]:=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_d}p_d(s)g(s).$$
The random sample is the subset $S\in\mathcal S_d$; probability and
expectation here average over the design while holding every $y_i$ fixed.

For $i,j\in U$, define the **inclusion indicator**
$$I_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&i\in s,\\0,&i\notin s,\end{cases}$$
the **first-order inclusion probability**
$$\pi_i:=P_d(\{s\in\mathcal S_d:i\in s\}),$$
and the **second-order inclusion probability**
$$\pi_{ij}:=P_d(\{s\in\mathcal S_d:i,j\in s\}).$$
In particular, $\pi_{ii}=\pi_i$.

The observed record includes the selected unit labels and their values. For a
common record space set
$$\mathcal X_d:=\{(s,z):s\in\mathcal S_d,\ z:s\to\mathbb R\},\qquad \mathcal A_d:=\mathcal P(\mathcal X_d),$$
and for each $y\in\mathbb R^U$ define
$$O_y(s):=(s,y|_s),\qquad P_y^d(B):=\sum_{\substack{s\in\mathcal S_d\\O_y(s)\in B}}p_d(s)\quad(B\in\mathcal A_d).$$
For a real-valued statistic $h$ on $\mathcal X_d$, write
$$E_y^d[h]:=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_d}p_d(s)h(O_y(s))=E_d[h\circ O_y];$$
this is expectation under the induced observed-data law.
The local well-definedness result
[[lem-finite-population-design-law-is-a-probability-measure]] shows that each
$P_y^d$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X_d,\mathcal A_d)$. Hence
$$\mathsf E_d:=((\mathcal X_d,\mathcal A_d),\mathbb R^U,(P_y^d)_{y\in\mathbb R^U})$$
is a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), with parametric
model $\mathsf P_d(y)=P_y^d$ ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). The total
$y\mapsto T(y)$ and mean $y\mapsto\bar y_U$ are estimands
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

This is design probability: the $y_i$ are fixed and only $S$ is random. A
superpopulation model instead assigns a probability law to the values $y_i$;
that additional law is separate from $p_d$. The finite-population target and
the sampling unit must be recorded in the scientific model contract
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]). In fixed-design regression,
the matrix $X$ is held fixed and has no selection law; that convention alone
does not specify a sampling design on $U$
([[def-fixed-design-linear-regression-model]]).

Let $(U,y)$ be a finite population with a sampling design as in
[[def-finite-population-and-sampling-design]]. For each ordered pair
$(i,j)\in U\times U$, the **inclusion-covariance difference** is
$$\Delta_{ij}:=\pi_{ij}-\pi_i\pi_j,$$
where $\pi_i$ is the probability that unit $i$ is included and $\pi_{ij}$ is
the probability that both $i$ and $j$ are included. The supplier convention
$\pi_{ii}=\pi_i$ gives $\Delta_{ii}=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$.

Let $(U,y)$ be a finite population with a fixed-size sampling design as in
[[def-finite-population-and-sampling-design]], so every supported sample has
the same size $n$. Assume $\pi_i>0$ for every $i\in U$ and put
$x_i:=y_i/\pi_i$. Then
$$\sum_{j\in U}\Delta_{ij}=0\quad(i\in U),$$
and the Horvitz–Thompson variance satisfies the Sen–Yates–Grundy identity
$$\operatorname{Var}_d(\widehat T_{HT})=-\frac12\sum_{i,j\in U}\Delta_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2.$$
If additionally $\pi_{ij}>0$ for every ordered pair, then the sample
expression
$$\widehat V_{SYG}:=-\frac12\sum_{i,j\in U}I_iI_j\frac{\Delta_{ij}}{\pi_{ij}}(x_i-x_j)^2$$
is unbiased for $\operatorname{Var}_d(\widehat T_{HT})$. If
$\Delta_{ij}\le0$ for every distinct pair, this condition guarantees that
$\widehat V_{SYG}$ is nonnegative for every supported sample. It is a
sufficient sign condition for the sample expression; the true variance in
the identity is nonnegative for every valid design.

For $y^A=(0,0,1,1)$, $x=(0,0,2,2)$. Samples $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ give SYG estimate zero; each cross sample gives $-\Delta_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2/\pi_{ij}=16$. $$\prod_{h=1}^H\binom{N_h}{n_h}^{-1},$$
and its sample in $U$ is $R=\bigcup_{h=1}^H r_h$. This is the
**stratified SRSWOR design**. The union map is one-to-one because the strata
are disjoint; the support has $\prod_h\binom{N_h}{n_h}$ elements, so the
displayed mass function sums to one.

The fixed mean in stratum $h$ is
$$\bar y_h=\frac1{N_h}\sum_{i\in U_h}y_i.$$
For a noncertainty stratum ($n_h<N_h$), necessarily $N_h>1$, and its finite-
population variance is
$$S_h^2=\frac1{N_h-1}\sum_{i\in U_h}(y_i-\bar y_h)^2.$$
For every noncertainty stratum write $S_h=\sqrt{S_h^2}$ for its nonnegative
population standard deviation. For a realized sample, set
$$\bar y_{h,R}=\frac1{n_h}\sum_{i\in R_h}y_i,\qquad \widehat T_{st}=\sum_{h=1}^H N_h\bar y_{h,R}.$$

$n_h=N_h$, the stratum is a certainty stratum and its contribution is the
fixed total $N_h\bar y_h$; no $S_h^2$ is needed for that term. The population
values $y_i$ remain fixed: only the sample selections are random.

design probability $P_d$, the stratified total estimator satisfies
$$E_d[\widehat T_{st}]=\sum_{i\in U}y_i.$$

$$\operatorname{Var}_d(\widehat T_{st})=\sum_{h:n_h<N_h}N_h^2\left(1-\frac{n_h}{N_h}\right)\frac{S_h^2}{n_h}.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

Equivalently, it is
$\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

derivations.claim: The positive-weight support is nonempty by [F1]. List its finitely many distinct score values in decreasing order as $t_1>\cdots>t_m$, let $d_j=\sum_{T(\omega)=t_j}w(\omega)>0$, and put $a_0=0$ and $a_j=\sum_{k=1}^j d_k$. These cumulative masses satisfy $0=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_m=1$.

If $T(Z)=t_j$, then $q(Z)=a_j$. For $u<1$, the indices with $a_j\le u$ form an initial segment; if its last index is $j_0$, then $\Pr(q(Z)\le u)=\sum_{j\le j_0}d_j=a_{j_0}\le u$, while an empty segment has probability zero. At $u=1$ the probability is one. Thus $q(Z)$ is superuniform.

On the score level $t_j$, the strict-tail mass is $a_{j-1}$ and the tied mass is $d_j$, so $q^+(Z,U)=a_{j-1}+Ud_j$. By [A1], conditional on this score level its probability of being at most $u$ is zero for $u\le a_{j-1}$, $(u-a_{j-1})/d_j$ for $a_{j-1}<u<a_j$, and one for $u\ge a_j$.

Multiplying these conditional probabilities by $d_j$ gives the lengths of $[a_{j-1},a_j]\cap[0,u]$. These consecutive intervals partition $[0,1]$, so their lengths sum to $u$. Therefore $\Pr(q^+(Z,U)\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent. Their values are
**substantively untestable** from the observed-data law; the
assignment-invariance claim is a hypothesis tested by the theorem, not an
empirical fact supplied by the design. These classifications do not make
the design or scientific model empirically true.

In the finite randomized treatment-assignment model
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]], a schedule satisfies
the **Fisher sharp null** when for each unit $i$ there is a value $y_i$ such that
$Y_i(z)=y_i$ for every allowed assignment $z$. The full vector
$y=(y_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$ is then imputable under every assignment.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:
assignment $z'$ is at least as extreme as $z$ when $T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)$.
For a signed score $S$ and fixed null center $s_0$, the corresponding
two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$; for a no-effect
sharp null the center is $s_0=0$. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data
sigma-algebra makes every such real-valued map measurable.

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space, let $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$,
and let $Z$ have law $w$. Define
$$q(z):=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)1\{T(\omega)\ge T(z)\}.$$
Then $\Pr(q(Z)\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$. If an auxiliary random
variable $U$ is independent of $Z$ and uniform on $[0,1]$, define
$$q^+(Z,U):=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)1\{T(\omega)>T(Z)\}+U\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)1\{T(\omega)=T(Z)\}.$$
Then $\Pr(q^+(Z,U)\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Consider the no-interference binary-treatment submodel of
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]] in which the allowed
assignment set is $\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ and unit $i$'s response under
assignment vector $z$ is $Y_i(z)=Y_i(z_i)$ for fixed real potential responses
$Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1)$. For the fixed units, define the
**finite-population average treatment effect** by
$$\tau_F:=\frac1N\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\bigr).$$
The **weak zero-average-effect null** is the hypothesis $\tau_F=0$; it
constrains the average of the unit-level effects, not each effect separately.
The Fisher sharp null in this submodel, defined in
[[def-fisher-sharp-null-and-predeclared-test-orderings]], requires
$Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)$ for every unit. No probability distribution on the fixed
potential responses is part of either definition.

derivations.claim: The schedule with $Y_i(z)=0$ for every unit and assignment belongs to the Fisher sharp null, so its null class is nonempty as required by [F4]. Fix any sharp-null schedule $\theta$ and choose its common response vector $y$ by [F2]. For every realized assignment $Z$, the observed vector $Y_\theta(Z)$ equals $y$, and every assignment score $T(z,y)$ is therefore imputable.

The formula $p_{\rm rand}(z,y)$ is a finite sum of selected nonnegative assignment weights, so it lies in $[0,1]$. It is a statistic because the data space has its full power-set sigma-algebra, so every preimage is measurable by [F5]. On the product extension with law $\widetilde P_\theta=P_\theta\otimes\lambda$, $p^+$ is a finite combination of score comparisons on the finite assignment space and the measurable coordinate $U$, so it is measurable and its value lies between zero and the total assignment mass one.

On this fixed schedule set $T_y(z)=T(z,y)$. Substituting $Y_\theta(Z)=y$ from step 1.1 into the two displayed formulas identifies $p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ and $p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)$ with the two finite weighted rank transforms of [F3] on $(\mathcal Z,p)$, using [A1] for the tie-randomized transform. Hence $P_\theta(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u)\le u$ and $\widetilde P_\theta(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Since the bound holds for every schedule in the sharp null, [F4] makes $p_{\rm rand}$ a valid p-value for that null. The randomized value is uniform under each extended law $\widetilde P_\theta$, and therefore is also superuniform there; its threshold rule has null rejection probability at most its threshold. No step uses an error distribution. By [F2] and [F6], the argument covers a weak average-effect schedule only when it also satisfies the sharp null.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: The model requires a nonempty assignment space, and the sharp-null parameter class is nonempty because constant outcome schedules exist.
Statement: Zero-weight assignments are permitted by the model, appear with zero contribution in the weighted sums, and require no division.
Statement: A singleton assignment law reduces to the one-score case of [F3], giving $p_{\rm rand}=1$ and $p^+=U$.
Statement: If all positive-probability assignments have the same score, the inclusive p-value is one and randomized ties give the supplied uniform variable.
Statement: The theorem and [F3] include $u=0$ and $u=1$; the inclusive p-value bound holds at both endpoints.
Statement: The reduction uses only the finite assignment space, fixed schedule, and finite weighted-tail lemma. It assumes no choice axiom.

In the finite randomized treatment-assignment model
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]], a schedule satisfies
the **Fisher sharp null** when for each unit $i$ there is a value $y_i$ such that
$Y_i(z)=y_i$ for every allowed assignment $z$. The full vector
$y=(y_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$ is then imputable under every assignment.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:
assignment $z'$ is at least as extreme as $z$ when $T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)$.
For a signed score $S$ and fixed null center $s_0$, the corresponding
two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$; for a no-effect
sharp null the center is $s_0=0$. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data
sigma-algebra makes every such real-valued map measurable.

In a finite randomized treatment-assignment model, fix any real-valued
predeclared ordering score $T(z,y)$. For observed data $(z,y)$ define
$$p_{\rm rand}(z,y):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)\}.$$
Let $\lambda$ be the uniform probability measure on $[0,1]$. For each
$\theta$, use the product extension of the data experiment with law
$\widetilde P_\theta:=P_\theta\otimes\lambda$, and let $U$ be its
$[0,1]$ coordinate. Define
$$p^+(z,y,U):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)>T(z,y)\}+U\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)=T(z,y)\}.$$
For every schedule satisfying the Fisher sharp null and every
$u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_\theta\!\left(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u\right)\le u,$$
whereas the added randomization gives
$$\widetilde P_\theta\!\left(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u\right)=u.$$

and randomized ties give an exactly uniform p-value when the additional
independent uniform randomizer is used. For a two-sided test, take
$T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$ with its center $s_0$ fixed in advance. The result
uses the actual, possibly unequal assignment probabilities; random
assignment supplies no Gaussian error law, and this theorem makes no
validity claim under the weak zero-average-effect null from
[[def-finite-population-average-treatment-effect-and-weak-null]] unless it
is also Fisher-sharp.

derivations.claim: The assignment weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and each unit's outcome is the same under all three assignments, so this is a finite assignment law satisfying the Fisher sharp null.
If unit 1, 2, or 3 is treated, the signed differences are respectively $0-(1+2)/2=-3/2$, $1-(0+2)/2=0$, and $2-(0+1)/2=3/2$. The two-sided scores are therefore $3/2,0,3/2$.

Each outer assignment has inclusive upper-tail mass $1/2+1/6=2/3$; the middle score is the minimum, so its inclusive upper-tail mass is $1$. The nonrandomized p-value therefore equals $2/3$ with probability $2/3$ and $1$ with probability $1/3$. Its distribution function is $0$ below $2/3$, $2/3$ on $[2/3,1)$, and $1$ at $1$, which is at most its argument throughout $[0,1]$.

At either outer assignment the strict-tail mass is zero and the tied mass is $2/3$, so $p^+=(2/3)U$. At the middle assignment the strict-tail mass is $2/3$ and the tied mass is $1/3$, so $p^+=2/3+U/3$.

For $0\le u\le2/3$, the outer assignments contribute $(2/3)P(U\le 3u/2)=u$. For $2/3\le u\le1$, they contribute $2/3$ and the middle assignment contributes $(1/3)P(U\le3u-2)=u-2/3$; hence $P(p^+\le u)=u$ on the entire unit interval. Together with step 3.1, this verifies the theorem's superuniform and uniform conclusions for this assignment law.

same $t$ fixed experimental units, indexed within block $j$ by
$i\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$. The $t$ treatments form a fixed set $\mathcal T$ with
$|\mathcal T|=t$. A **complete block** is a block in which each treatment is
assigned to exactly one unit. The blocks and their units are fixed before
randomization.

Let $S_t$ be the set of permutations from the unit labels to $\mathcal T$.
The **randomized complete-block design (RCBD)** uses assignment space
$\mathcal Z=(S_t)^b$ and the uniform probability law on this finite nonempty
set. Thus each $z=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_b)$ has probability $(t!)^{-b}$; the
within-block treatment permutations are independent and individually uniform.
This is a finite randomized-treatment assignment model
([[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]]) whose units are the
$tb$ cells and whose assignment is the only randomness supplied by the
design. The design specifies no response model, Gaussian errors, additivity,
or absence of interference. A pair is the special case $t=2,b=1$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $V$ be a vector
space over $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $U$ be a family of linear subspaces
$U_i$ of $V$ indexed by $i < n$ ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]) with

$$V \;=\; \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$$

([[def-internal-direct-sum]]) and every $U_i$ finite-dimensional over $F$
([[def-dimension]]). Then $V$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and

$$\dim_F V \;=\; \sum_{i<n} \dim_F U_i ,$$

the right-hand side being the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read
additively in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{N}, +, 0)$
([[def-nat-addition]], [[lem-nat-add-identity]],
[[lem-nat-add-associative]], [[lem-nat-add-commutative]]).

**The base case is a genuine case.** At $n = 0$ the direct sum of the empty
family is $\{0_V\}$ and the empty sum of natural numbers is $0$, so the formula
reads $\dim_F\{0_V\} = 0$. **At $n = 2$** it reads
$\dim_F(U \oplus W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$.

**No choice principle is used.** The only inputs are
[[thm-dimension-formula]] and [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], both of
which are proved in finite dimension without one.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$. Its **row space** $\operatorname{Row}(A)\subseteq F^n$ is the span of its rows, its **column space** $\operatorname{Col}(A)\subseteq F^m$ is the span of its columns, and its **nullspace** is
$$N(A):=\{x\in F^n:Ax=0\}.$$

The **row rank** and **column rank** are
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Row}(A),\qquad \operatorname{crank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Col}(A).$$
These dimensions are defined because each space is spanned by a finite list.
Starting with the empty list, inspect the spanning vectors in order and retain a
vector exactly when it is not in the span of those already retained. Induction
shows that the retained list is independent and has the same span as the
original finite list, so it is a finite basis. The **rank** of $A$ is its row
rank; [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] proves that it also equals the column
rank.

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

For every $a\in\mathbb R^t$, the vector $h=a-(\mathbf1_t^Ta/t)\mathbf1_t$ lies in $H$ and satisfies $Ch=Ca$, because $C\mathbf1_t=0$. Thus $\operatorname{im}(C|_H)=\operatorname{im}C$ has dimension $q$, and [F2] gives $\dim(H\cap\ker C)=t-1-q$. The row space of $C$ lies in $H$ and is orthogonal to $H\cap\ker C$. The orthogonal complement of $H\cap\ker C$ within $H$ has dimension $q$: both subspaces are finite-dimensional by [F4], and [F3]–[F5] subtract dimensions from $\dim H=t-1$. Since this complement contains the $q$-dimensional row space, the equality case of [F4] identifies it with that row space.

In $V$, the constant arrays form a one-dimensional space $G$, the arrays $(a_i)_{ij}$ for $a\in H$ form a $(t-1)$-dimensional treatment space $T$, and the arrays $(d_j)_{ij}$ for $d\in\mathbb R^b$ with $\sum_jd_j=0$ form a $(b-1)$-dimensional block space $B$. The replication maps from the two zero-sum coordinate spaces to $T$ and $B$ are linear bijections: their repeated rows or columns recover the original coordinates, so they transport bases and give the stated dimensions; the block zero-sum space has dimension $b-1$ by [F2] applied to its onto coordinate-sum map. These spaces are pairwise orthogonal: the treatment-block inner product is $\sum_{i,j}a_id_j=(\sum_i a_i)(\sum_jd_j)=0$, and either zero-sum condition also makes the relevant inner product with $G$ zero. Their sum is direct: if three mutually orthogonal vectors sum to zero, taking the inner product with each one gives its squared norm zero. Thus $W_U=G\oplus T\oplus B$, and the finite-dimensional direct-sum formula [F5] gives $\dim W_U=1+(t-1)+(b-1)=t+b-1$. The reduced space replaces $T$ by the replicated arrays from $H\cap\ker C$, whose dimension is $t-1-q$ by step 1.1; the same formula gives $\dim W_R(C)=1+(t-1-q)+(b-1)=t+b-1-q$.

For any $y$, set $r_{ij}=y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot j}+\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$. Summing $r$ over any row gives zero because $\sum_j y_{ij}=b\bar y_{i\cdot}$ and $\sum_j\bar y_{\cdot j}=b\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$; summing over any column likewise gives zero. Conversely, if $v$ is orthogonal to $T$, then its row-sum vector is orthogonal to every $a\in H$, so all row sums are equal; orthogonality to $G$ makes their total zero, so every row sum is zero. The same argument with $B$ gives zero column sums. Thus $W_U^\perp=E$. Also $(y-r)_{ij}=\bar y_{i\cdot}+\bar y_{\cdot j}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$ belongs to $W_U$. By [F3], this is the orthogonal decomposition of $y$ relative to $W_U$, proving the formula for $RSS_U$; the subspace $E$ is finite-dimensional by [F4], and [F3] gives $V=W_U\oplus E$. Since the standard cell-coordinate basis makes $\dim V=tb$, [F5] gives $\dim E=tb-(t+b-1)=(t-1)(b-1)$.

Put $P_C=C^T(CC^T)^{-1}C$. The matrix $CC^T$ is invertible since $C$ has full row rank. Direct multiplication gives $P_C^T=P_C$, $P_C^2=P_C$, and image $P_C=\operatorname{row}(C)$. For any $x$ and $a\in\mathbb R^q$, $\langle x-P_Cx,C^Ta\rangle=a^TCx-a^TCC^T(CC^T)^{-1}Cx=0$, so [F3] identifies $P_C$ as the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{row}(C)$. Consequently $T$ is the orthogonal direct sum of the reduced treatment space and the treatment arrays formed from $\operatorname{row}(C)$. Therefore $W_U=W_R(C)\oplus D_C$, where $D_C=\{(a_i)_{ij}:a\in\operatorname{row}(C)\}$.

The projection of $y$ onto $D_C$ is the array repeating $P_C\bar y$ across all $b$ blocks: its residual is orthogonal to every repeated $a\in\operatorname{row}(C)$ because the inner product is $b\,a^T(\bar y-P_C\bar y)=0$. Its squared norm is $b\|P_C\bar y\|^2=b(C\bar y)^T(CC^T)^{-1}(C\bar y)$. In the orthogonal direct sum of step 3.2, $y-P_{W_R}y$ is this projection plus $y-P_{W_U}y$, and the two parts are orthogonal; expanding the squared norm gives the claimed residual-sum reduction.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,

derivations.claim: Let $S=\delta_1$ when unit $1$ receives treatment $1$ and $S=\delta_2$ when unit $2$ receives it. These outcomes have weights $1/2$ by [F3]. Under assignment $(1,0)$, fix $Y_1(1)$ and $Y_2(0)$ but change $Y_1(0)$; the observed data stay the same while $S=Y_1(1)-Y_1(0)$ changes. derivations.claim: Write the cell array as $Y=m+\gamma+\epsilon$, where $m\in W_U$ is additive and $\gamma\in E$. By [F1], the residual from projection onto $W_U$ is $(I-P_{W_U})Y=\gamma+(I-P_{W_U})\epsilon$, and the latter error projection lies in $E=W_U^\perp$.

For any $h\in E$, the identity $\gamma+(I-P_{W_U})\epsilon=(\gamma+h)+((I-P_{W_U})\epsilon-h)$ gives two decompositions of the same observed residual into vectors in $E$. Thus the cell data alone do not distinguish the unrestricted interaction component from the projected error component.

The additive space has dimension $t+b-1$ and $E$ has dimension $(t-1)(b-1)$, so their orthogonal direct sum has dimension $tb$, the full cell-space dimension. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n>p\ge1$ whose $p$ columns are linearly independent. Use the experiment on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ indexed by $(\beta,\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^p\times(0,\infty)$, with observation $Y=X\beta+\varepsilon$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Define the least-squares statistic and residual sum of squares by
$$\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY,\qquad P_X=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad RSS_X=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad S^2=\frac{RSS_X}{n-p},\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
For every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$\widetilde T_c:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{S\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-p},\qquad \frac{RSS_X}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-p}^2,$$
and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$, with $S>0$ almost surely.

For nested deterministic full and reduced design spaces $W_R\subset W_U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of dimensions $p-q$ and $p$, where $q$ is an integer and $1\le q\le p<n$, let $P_R,P_U$ be the orthogonal projections onto these spaces and define $RSS_R=\|(I-P_R)Y\|^2$ and $RSS_U=\|(I-P_U)Y\|^2$. Under the null hypothesis that the mean vector belongs to $W_R$,
$$\widetilde F:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q}{RSS_U/(n-p)},&RSS_U>0,\\ 0,&RSS_U=0 \end{cases} \sim F_{q,n-p}.$$
The numerator and denominator chi-square contributions are independent. All t and F denominator degrees of freedom in the statement are positive.

$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k\le0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s\le0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$ and are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the complementary Borel nonpositive-denominator region is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map

and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.

does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Fix $t\ge1$ and put $R_t=\{0,1,\ldots,t-1\}$, with addition interpreted
modulo $t$. A **Latin-square allocation of order $t$** is a function
$L:R_t\times R_t\to R_t$ such that for
each fixed row the map from columns to treatments is a bijection, and for
each fixed column the map from rows to treatments is a bijection. Thus each
treatment occurs exactly once in every row and every column. Let
$\mathcal L_t$ be the finite set of these allocations and assign the uniform
law on $\mathcal L_t$. This law is well-defined: $L_0(r,c)=r+c\pmod t$ is a

$\mathcal L_t$ is nonempty. This specifies one exact
restricted randomization law. It randomizes over treatment-by-row-by-column
assignments and, for $t\ge2$, is distinct from the product of independent
within-block permutations in an RCBD ([[def-randomized-complete-block-design]]).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $t,b\ge2$ and observe one real response $Y_{ij}$ for each treatment $i$
and block $j$. In the additive mean model, the residual subspace consists of
the double-centered arrays
$$E=\{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{t\times b}:\sum_j\gamma_{ij}=0\ \text{for every }i,\ \sum_i\gamma_{ij}=0\ \text{for every }j\},$$
which has dimension $(t-1)(b-1)$ ([[lem-rcbd-nested-contrast-model-and-projection]]).
If a treatment-by-block interaction $\gamma\in E$ is included in the mean,
then the additive-fit residual is $\gamma+P_E\epsilon$, where $P_E\epsilon$
is the projection of the cell error onto $E$. For every $h\in E$ this same
residual equals $(\gamma+h)+(P_E\epsilon-h)$. Hence one observation per cell
does not separately decompose the realized residual into unrestricted
interaction and projected error, and fitting the unrestricted interaction
leaves zero pure-error residual degrees of freedom. This is an algebraic
design limitation; it does not assert nonidentifiability under every
additional stochastic model.

Consider one pair in the $t=2,b=1$ RCBD, with the two treatments labelled
$0$ and $1$. Let $Y_\ell(z)\in\mathbb R$ be unit $\ell$'s fixed potential
outcome under its own treatment $z\in\{0,1\}$, and assume no interference:
the outcome depends on the pair assignment only through that unit's own
treatment. Define $\delta_\ell=Y_\ell(1)-Y_\ell(0)$,
$\tau=(\delta_1+\delta_2)/2$, and the two possible observed contrasts
$$D_1=Y_1(1)-Y_2(0),\qquad D_2=Y_2(1)-Y_1(0).$$
If exactly one unit is assigned treatment $1$ uniformly at random, the
observed treated-minus-control contrast $D$ obeys
$$\mathbb E_d[D]=\tau,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_d(D)=\frac{(D_1-D_2)^2}{4}=\frac{\bigl((\delta_1-\delta_2)+2(Y_1(0)-Y_2(0))\bigr)^2}{4}.$$
Here $\mathbb E_d$ and $\operatorname{Var}_d$ average over treatment
assignment only, holding all potential outcomes fixed. The variance depends
on baseline outcomes as well as effect heterogeneity.

In the two-unit, two-treatment paired randomization, let
$\delta_\ell=Y_\ell(1)-Y_\ell(0)$ and
$\tau=(\delta_1+\delta_2)/2$. Define $S$ to be the fixed treatment effect
$\delta_\ell$ of whichever unit $\ell$ is assigned treatment $1$. Then
$$\mathbb E_d[S]=\tau,\qquad \operatorname{Var}_d(S)=\frac{(\delta_1-\delta_2)^2}{4}.$$
The random variable $S$ uses both potential outcomes of the selected unit;
it is not the observed treated-minus-control contrast and is not a statistic
of the observed outcomes.

$$\mathcal X_k=\{-1,+1\}^{[k]},$$

$$x_A=\prod_{j\in A}x_j,$$
where the empty product is $x_\varnothing=1$. The design matrix $X$ has one row for each run, one column for each subset of factors, and entry $X_{x,A}=x_A$. Any fixed ordering of the runs and subsets may be used.

$$\widehat\beta_A(y)=2^{-k}\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_k}x_Ay_x.$$

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

Let $A$ be invertible. Then the inversion map is real Fr\'echet differentiable
at $A$, and for every direction $H$,

$$D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}.$$

$$D(\operatorname{tr})(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(H).$$

satisfies

By [F4], with its cofactor and adjugate support [F6], [F7], and [F8], $g_x'(0)=\operatorname{tr}((M^*)^{-1}(f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}-M^*))=u^*(x)-p$; the trace of the rank-one term is $f(x)^{\mathsf T}(M^*)^{-1}f(x)$ by the coordinate sum, and $\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p$ by [F5]. Thus $u^*(x)\le p$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, the pointwise bound is necessary.

For a differentiable concave function, $g(1)-g(0)\le g'(0)$ because its derivative is nonincreasing on $[0,1]$. Step 1.2 therefore gives $\log\det N\le\log\det M^*$. Since $\eta$ was arbitrary among nonsingular designs, $\xi^*$ is D-optimal.

Finally, $\sum_x\xi_x^*u^*(x)=\operatorname{tr}((M^*)^{-1}\sum_x\xi_x^*f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p$ by [F1] and [F5]. Each term is at most $p$ by the bound assumed in step 1.2, so every term with $\xi_x^*>0$ equals $p$. This proves equality on the support and completes both directions.
