citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Every second-countable locally compact Hausdorff space is Polish,
hence standard Borel. Consequently, if $G$ is a second-countable locally
compact Hausdorff topological group and $H\le G$ is a closed subgroup, then
the homogeneous space $G/H$ with its quotient topology is Polish and the
quotient Borel structure together with the left action
$G\times G/H\to G/H$ is a standard Borel $G$-space with Borel action.

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

A topological space $(X, \mathcal{T})$ ([[def-topological-space]]) is **locally
compact** when

> every point of $X$ has a compact neighbourhood:

that is, for every $x \in X$ there is a neighbourhood $N$ of $x$
([[def-neighbourhood-top]]) that is a compact subset of $X$
([[def-compact-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**A neighbourhood need not be open here**, and that is what makes the condition
the weak one it is meant to be: $N$ is required only to contain some open set
containing $x$. Writing "compact **open** neighbourhood" instead would define a
strictly stronger property, satisfied by no space in which a point has no compact
open neighbourhood, $\mathbb{R}$ among them; and requiring the compact set merely
to *contain* $x$ would define a property so weak that every space with a
singleton has it, singletons being compact.

**Every compact space is locally compact**, since $X$ itself is a neighbourhood
of each of its points and is a compact subset of itself. The converse fails, and
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is the standard witness.

**What the condition says in a metric space.** Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
carrying its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metrizable-space]]),
with balls as in [[def-metric-ball]], and let $x \in X$. Then

> $x$ has a compact neighbourhood **if and only if** there are a real $r > 0$ and
> a compact $K \subseteq X$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq K$.

*Both directions are immediate and are discharged here.* If $N$ is a compact
neighbourhood of $x$, fix an open $U$ with $x \in U \subseteq N$; by
[[def-metric-topology]] there is $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U \subseteq N$, so
$K := N$ serves. Conversely, if $B(x,r) \subseteq K$ with $K$ compact, then $K$
contains the open set $B(x,r)$, which contains $x$, so $K$ is a neighbourhood of
$x$ and is compact. Compactness of a subset of $(X,d)$ means the same thing read
metrically and read topologically
([[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]]), so the criterion may be
applied with either development's theorems.

**$\mathbb{R}^n$ is locally compact for every $n \ge 1$.** Give $\mathbb{R}^n$
the product topology, which is the metric topology of the Euclidean metric $d_2$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[cor-heine-borel-in-the-product-topology]]). For
$p \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the set

$$Q_p \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : d_2(x,p) \le 1 \,\}$$

is closed, being the complement of the union of the open balls $B(y, d_2(y,p) - 1)$
over the points $y$ with $d_2(y,p) > 1$, and it is bounded
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]), lying inside $B(p, 2)$; so $Q_p$ is compact by
[[cor-heine-borel-in-the-product-topology]]. It contains the open ball $B(p,1)$,
which contains $p$, so it is a compact neighbourhood of $p$. The space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is not compact, so local compactness is strictly weaker than
compactness.

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces. A family
$(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, indexed by all finite subsets of $I$, is a **consistent family of finite-dimensional
distributions** when each $\mu_F$ is a probability measure on
$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$, with the finite unordered product
sigma-algebra of [[def-coordinate-maps-and-cylinder-sigma-algebra]], and for
every pair of finite sets $F\subseteq G\subseteq I$ the pushforward of
$\mu_G$ under the restriction $p_{G,F}(x)=x|_F$ equals $\mu_F$; equivalently,
$\mu_G(p_{G,F}^{-1}(A))=\mu_F(A)$ for every
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The restriction is measurable since
inverse images of coordinate generators are coordinate generators. The empty
support carries the unique probability measure on the singleton empty product.

Reordering means choosing a different enumeration of the **same** finite set
$F$. If $e:[n]\to F$ is an enumeration, its displayed ordered law is the
pushforward of $\mu_F$ under $r_e(x)=(x_{e(0)},\ldots,x_{e(n-1)})$.
For another enumeration $e'$, the coordinate permutation $r_{e'}\circ r_e^{-1}$
pushes this ordered law to the one displayed using $e'$. This is automatic
from these definitions and does not require equal laws on different subsets
of $I$, or invariance under permutations of a fixed ordered product.
In particular, consistency is data about
every finite joint law, not merely the one-coordinate marginals.

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

Let $T\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, have its relative Borel sigma-algebra, and
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be one probability space. A **real random
field** indexed by $T$ is a family $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ of real random variables
$X(s):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on that space. This is coordinate measurability:
each map $(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ with $s$ fixed is measurable in
$\omega$. The field is **jointly measurable** when the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ from
$(T\times\Omega,\mathcal B(T)\otimes\mathcal F)$ to
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Joint measurability is an
additional hypothesis when a spatial Lebesgue integral is used; it is not part
of coordinate measurability.

Write $\mathcal L(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))$ for the pushforward law of a finite
coordinate tuple ([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). The field is **strictly stationary** on $T$ when, for every
finite tuple $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$ and every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ for which
$s_i+u\in T$ for all $i$, these joint laws are invariant under the common
translation $s_i\mapsto s_i+u$. This extends the integer-shift convention for
time series in [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] to spatial
indices.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs
of sites.

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its
mean is one constant $m$, and there is a function $C:T-T\to\mathbb R$ such
that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$
For a wide-stationary field on all of $\mathbb R^d$, it is **wide isotropic**
when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put
$\Delta_hX(s):=X(s+h)-X(s)$. The field is **intrinsically stationary of order
two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of
$\Delta_hX(s)$ are finite and independent of the admissible starting site
$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

derivations.claim: For each nonempty finite $F\subseteq T$, use AC to choose an enumeration $e_F:\{1,\ldots,n_F\}\to F$. Put $t_i=e_F(i)$, $m_F=(m(t_i))_{i=1}^{n_F}$, and $K_F=[K(t_i,t_j)]_{i,j=1}^{n_F}$. Let $r_F:\mathbb R^{n_F}\to\mathbb R^F$ relabel coordinates by $r_F(x)(e_F(i))=x_i$. The matrix $K_F$ is symmetric positive semidefinite by the hypothesis on $K$, so [F1] supplies $N_{n_F}(m_F,K_F)$; define the probability measure on the actual coordinate space by $\mu_F:=(r_F)_\#N_{n_F}(m_F,K_F)$. If $F=\varnothing$, use the unique probability law on the singleton empty product. Changing the enumeration permutes $m_F$ and both indices of $K_F$ by the same permutation. The characteristic-function formula in [F2] shows that the corresponding permutation of $\mathbb R^{n_F}$ carries one Gaussian law to the other; after relabelling, the resulting measure on $\mathbb R^F$ is unchanged. Thus $\mu_F$ is independent of the chosen enumeration.

The intervals $(p,q)$ with rational endpoints form a countable family by the countability of $\mathbb Q$ and [F4]. They form a base: if $U$ is open and $x\in U$, choose $r>0$ with $(x-r,x+r)\subseteq U$; rational density supplies $p,q\in\mathbb Q$ with $x-r<p<x<q<x+r$, so $x\in(p,q)\subseteq U$. Thus $\mathbb R$ is second-countable by [F4]. If $x\ne y$, the open balls about $x$ and $y$ of radius $|x-y|/3$ are disjoint: a point in both would give $|x-y|<2|x-y|/3$ by the triangle inequality. Hence the metric topology is Hausdorff. It is locally compact since each $x$ has the compact interval $[x-1,x+1]$ as a neighborhood by [F4]. Therefore [F3] makes $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ standard Borel.

Let $F\subseteq H$ be finite and nonempty, and use the enumerations fixed in step 1.1. Write $\pi_{H,F}:\mathbb R^H\to\mathbb R^F$ for restriction. Let $T\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, have its relative Borel sigma-algebra, and
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be one probability space. A **real random
field** indexed by $T$ is a family $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ of real random variables
$X(s):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on that space. This is coordinate measurability:
each map $(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ with $s$ fixed is measurable in
$\omega$. The field is **jointly measurable** when the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ from
$(T\times\Omega,\mathcal B(T)\otimes\mathcal F)$ to
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Joint measurability is an
additional hypothesis when a spatial Lebesgue integral is used; it is not part
of coordinate measurability.

Write $\mathcal L(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))$ for the pushforward law of a finite
coordinate tuple ([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). The field is **strictly stationary** on $T$ when, for every
finite tuple $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$ and every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ for which
$s_i+u\in T$ for all $i$, these joint laws are invariant under the common
translation $s_i\mapsto s_i+u$. This extends the integer-shift convention for
time series in [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] to spatial
indices.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs
of sites.

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its
mean is one constant $m$, and there is a function $C:T-T\to\mathbb R$ such
that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$
For a wide-stationary field on all of $\mathbb R^d$, it is **wide isotropic**
when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put
$\Delta_hX(s):=X(s+h)-X(s)$. The field is **intrinsically stationary of order
two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of
$\Delta_hX(s)$ are finite and independent of the admissible starting site
$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$

derivations.claim: Suppose first that $X$ is wide stationary. For every $s,h$, its increments have mean zero because the field mean is constant. Wide stationarity gives $C(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(s+h))$ and $C(-h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X(s+h),X(s))$; covariance symmetry [F3] therefore gives $C(-h)=C(h)$. Both level variances equal $C(0)$, and the cross-covariance in the increment variance is $C(-h)=C(h)$. Thus $$\mathbb E[(X(s+h)-X(s))^2]=\operatorname{Var}(X(s+h)-X(s))=2C(0)-2C(h).$$ Dividing by two gives $\gamma(h)=C(0)-C(h)$.

For arbitrary sites $s_1,\ldots,s_n$, set $Y_i:=X(s_i)-X(0)$. Each $Y_i$ is square-integrable by order-two intrinsic stationarity, since it is an increment from $0$ to $s_i$. [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$

complete Lebesgue measure. A **Van Hove sequence of spatial windows** is a
sequence $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ of bounded Borel sets

$0<|W_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, $|W_n|\to\infty$, and

measurable. Thus the window volume diverges while every fixed compact spatial
enlargement adds a negligible relative volume.

$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $1\le p\le\infty$. For real random variables whose classes lie in
$L^p(\mathbb P)$ as defined by [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
write $X_n\to X$ **in $L^p$** when
$$\|[X_n]-[X]\|_{L^p(\mathbb P)}\longrightarrow0.$$ 
For $p<\infty$, this norm is
$$\|[X_n]-[X]\|_{L^p(\mathbb P)}=\bigl(\mathbb E|X_n-X|^p\bigr)^{1/p};$$
for $p=\infty$, it is the essential-supremum norm. Thus the assertion concerns
almost-everywhere equivalence classes, not chosen representatives.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

derivations.claim: By [F11], Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is sigma-finite under the assumed $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Its restriction to $W_n$ is finite by [A1], and the probability measure has total mass $1$. Thus all measure factors used below satisfy the sigma-finiteness hypotheses of [F5] and [F6], including the unbounded lag-space factor in $W_n\times\mathbb R^d$. For every $s$, [F4] with $V=1$ gives $\mathbb E|X(s)|\le(\mathbb E[X(s)^2])^{1/2}=M<\infty$, where $M$ is constant by the stated first- and second-order stationarity. The map $(s,\omega)\mapsto |X(s,\omega)|$ is product-measurable; Tonelli [F5] gives $\mathbb E\int_{W_n}|X(s)|\,ds =\int_{W_n}\mathbb E|X(s)|\,ds\le M|W_n|<\infty.$ Therefore the sample path is absolutely integrable almost surely. Tonelli also makes the event where this integral is finite measurable; its probability is one. Applying Tonelli separately to $X^+$ and $X^-$ makes both section integrals measurable, and their difference on that event, extended by zero on its null complement as in [A2], is measurable.

Since $\int_{W_n}\mathbb E|X(s)|\,ds<\infty$, Fubini [F6] applies to $X$ on $W_n\times\Omega$. Its constant mean gives $\mathbb E[\bar X_{W_n}]=\frac1{|W_n|}\int_{W_n}\mathbb E[X(s)]\,ds =\frac1{|W_n|}\int_{W_n}\mu\,ds=\mu.$

Put $Z(s):=X(s)-\mu$. The rectangle-preimage argument in [F9] makes $(s,t,\omega)\mapsto Z(s,\omega)Z(t,\omega)$ product-measurable. By [F4], $\mathbb E|Z(s)Z(t)|\le C(0)$ for all $s,t$. Iterated Tonelli [F5] therefore gives a finite integral, at most $C(0)|W_n|^2$, of the absolute pair product over $W_n\times W_n\times\Omega$. Each $\Omega$-section is integrable by this bound, so Fubini [F6] makes $(s,t)\mapsto\mathbb E[Z(s)Z(t)]$ measurable; it equals $C(t-s)$ by [F2]. A second Fubini calculation yields $\mathbb E\bigl[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2\bigr] =\frac1{|W_n|^2}\int_{W_n}\int_{W_n}C(t-s)\,dt\,ds.$ This also proves $\bar X_{W_n}\in L^2$.

Define $q_n(h):=|W_n\cap(W_n-h)|/|W_n|$. The addition-measurability argument in [F9] makes $(s,h)\mapsto\mathbf1_{W_n}(s)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)$ product-measurable, so Tonelli [F5] gives measurability of its section integral $q_n$. Also $0\le q_n(h)\le1$. For fixed $h$, translation invariance [F7] gives $|W_n\setminus(W_n-h)|=|(W_n+h)\setminus W_n|.$ The latter is bounded by $|(W_n+\{0,h\})\setminus W_n|$, so the Van Hove condition [A1] implies $q_n(h)\to1$.

The product-measurable integrand $C(h)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)$ is absolutely integrable: Tonelli and [F9] give
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{W_n}|C(h)|\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)\,ds\,dh\le |W_n|\|C\|_1<\infty.$$
In the inner integral of step 1.3 set $h=t-s$; translation invariance [F7]
gives $\int_{W_n}C(t-s)\,dt=\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)\,dh$.
Fubini [F6] then yields
$$\mathbb E\bigl[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2\bigr] =\frac1{|W_n|^2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)|W_n\cap(W_n-h)|\,dh.$$
The overlap factor is the measure of those $s\in W_n$ for which $s+h\in W_n$.

Multiplying the formula in step 2.1 by $|W_n|$ gives $|W_n|\,\mathbb E[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2]=\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)q_n(h)\,dh.$ By [F10], the right side converges to $\int C(h)\,dh$ because $|C(h)q_n(h)|\le|C(h)|\in L^1$. It is therefore bounded; since $|W_n|\to\infty$, step 2.1 implies $\mathbb E[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2]\to0$.
The mean identity in step 1.2 and the second-moment limit in step 3.1 are exactly $L^2$ convergence to $\mu$ by [F8].

derivations.claim: The additive group of $\mathbb Z$ is abelian by [F1]. Coordinatewise addition on $\mathbb Z^d$ is associative and commutative, has the zero vector as identity, and sends $x$ to $-x$ coordinatewise as its inverse. Hence $\mathbb Z^d$ is an abelian group.

For distinct $x,y\in\mathbb Z^d$, the singleton sets $\{x\}$ and $\{y\}$ are disjoint open neighbourhoods by [F2], so the space is Hausdorff by [F6]. Each singleton $\{x\}$ is finite and hence compact by [F7]; it is an open neighbourhood of $x$ by [F2]. Thus the space is locally compact by [F8].

The product topology on $\mathbb Z^d\times\mathbb Z^d$ is discrete: for each pair $(x,y)$, the basic open set $\{x\}\times\{y\}$ is its singleton by [F2, F3]. Therefore coordinatewise addition $\mathbb Z^d\times\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb Z^d$ and inversion $\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb Z^d$ are continuous by [F4]. By [F5] the group is a topological group, and with step 1.2 it is locally compact Hausdorff abelian. Every map from $\mathbb Z^d$ is continuous by [F2, F4].

derivations.claim: For $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\in\mathbb T^d$, the formula for $\Psi(z)$ is a homomorphism because for $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z^d$, $\Psi(z)(k+\ell)=\prod_r z_r^{k_r+\ell_r} =\left(\prod_r z_r^{k_r}\right)\left(\prod_r z_r^{\ell_r}\right).$ It is continuous because its domain $\mathbb Z^d$ is discrete, so every preimage of an open set is open. Therefore $\Psi(z)\in\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$.

The map $\Psi$ is a group homomorphism because $\Psi(zz')(k)=\prod_r(z_rz'_r)^{k_r} =\left(\prod_rz_r^{k_r}\right)\left(\prod_r(z'_r)^{k_r}\right)$ by [F3] and commutativity of $\mathbb T$ [F4]. If $\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$, put $z_r:=\chi(e_r)$, where $e_r$ is the $r$th standard basis vector. Then $z_r\in\mathbb T$ by [F1], and the decomposition $k=\sum_r k_re_r$ together with homomorphism and power laws gives $\chi(k)=\prod_r z_r^{k_r}$. Thus $\chi=\Psi(z)$; also $z_r=\chi(e_r)$ recovers each coordinate uniquely, so $\Psi$ is bijective.

For each fixed $k$, the coordinate map $z\mapsto\Psi(z)(k)$ is a finite product of continuous integer-power maps on $\mathbb T$, hence continuous by [F4]. The product-topology criterion and [F2] then imply that $\Psi$ is continuous into $\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$.

The inverse map is $\chi\mapsto(\chi(e_1),\ldots,\chi(e_d))$. Each coordinate is continuous by [F2], so the inverse is continuous into the finite product $\mathbb T^d$. Thus $\Psi$ is a homeomorphism by [F5] and a group isomorphism by step 1.2 and the pointwise group law in [F1].

Give $\mathbb Z^d$ the discrete topology and let
$\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ be the multiplicative unit circle. The
map
$$\Psi:\mathbb T^d\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z^d},\qquad \Psi(z_1,\ldots,z_d)(k_1,\ldots,k_d):=\prod_{r=1}^d z_r^{k_r}$$
is a topological group isomorphism, where the dual has the compact-open
topology and $\mathbb T^d$ has the product topology.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of
$\mathbb C$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]) and the multiplication of
$\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$,
$\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

For any family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$, if every $X_i$ is $T_0$, respectively $T_1$, respectively Hausdorff, then $\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ is respectively $T_0$, $T_1$, respectively Hausdorff. The empty product is included.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: If $B_1,B_2,\ldots$ are pairwise disjoint Borel subsets of $\mathbb T^d$, then their images under the bijection $\Psi$ are pairwise disjoint Borel sets by [F1]. Hence $F\!\left(\bigcup_{m\ge1}B_m\right) =\mu\!\left(\bigcup_{m\ge1}\Psi(B_m)\right) =\sum_{m\ge1}\mu(\Psi(B_m)) =\sum_{m\ge1}F(B_m).$ Thus $F$ is a positive measure, and $F(\mathbb T^d)=\mu(\widehat{\mathbb Z^d})<\infty$.

For Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb T^d$ and $\varepsilon>0$, outer regularity of $\mu$ gives an open $U\supseteq\Psi(B)$ with $\mu(U)<\mu(\Psi(B))+\varepsilon$. Then $\Psi^{-1}(U)$ is open, contains $B$, and $F(\Psi^{-1}(U))=\mu(U)$, proving outer regularity of $F$. If $U$ is open in $\mathbb T^d$, inner regularity of $\mu$ gives compact $C\subseteq\Psi(U)$ with $\mu(C)>\mu(\Psi(U))-\varepsilon$. Then $\Psi^{-1}(C)$ is compact in $U$ and $F(\Psi^{-1}(C))=\mu(C)$, proving inner regularity on open sets. The torus is compact Hausdorff by [F4], so these properties make $F$ Radon as in [F2].

For an indicator $g=\mathbf1_B$ of a Borel set, $\int g\,dF=F(B)=\mu(\Psi(B)) =\int \mathbf1_B(\Psi^{-1}(\chi))\,\mu(d\chi).$ Finite linearity [F3] extends this equality to Borel simple functions. For a nonnegative Borel function $g$, the simple-approximation theorem [F3] supplies Borel simple functions $s_m\uparrow g$. Since $\Psi^{-1}$ is continuous, $s_m\circ\Psi^{-1}\uparrow g\circ\Psi^{-1}$ measurably on the dual. Applying monotone convergence [F3] to the simple-function identity on both spaces gives the asserted identity for $g$. Splitting the real and imaginary parts of a bounded complex Borel function into positive and negative parts then gives the stated identity by [F5].

derivations.claim: For any finite lattice points $k_1,\ldots,k_m\in\mathbb Z^d$ and complex coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_m$, the finite sum $\sum_r a_r(Y_{k_r}-\mu)$ is square-integrable. Expanding its squared modulus, using [F6] and stationarity, gives $\sum_{r,s}a_r\overline{a_s}c(k_r-k_s) =\mathbb E\left|\sum_r a_r(Y_{k_r}-\mu)\right|^2\ge0.$ Thus $c$ is positive definite by [F1].

By [F9], $\mathbb Z^d$ is a locally compact Hausdorff abelian group and every function on it is continuous, so $c$ is continuous. By Bochner's theorem [F2], using AC [A1] and DC [A2], there is a unique finite positive Radon measure $F_0$ on $\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}$ such that $c(h)=\int_{\widehat{\mathbb Z^d}}\chi(h)\,F_0(d\chi).$

Expand the finite squared modulus in [F5]. Every product is integrable by [F7], and stationarity gives $\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)] =\frac1{(2\pi)^dn^d}\sum_{j,k\in\Lambda_n} c(j-k)e^{-i(j-k)\cdot\lambda}.$

By [F3] and [F4], transport $F_0$ to the unique finite positive Radon measure $F$ on $\mathbb T^d$. Applying the integral-transport identity [F4] to $\chi\mapsto\chi(h)$ gives $c(h)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}e^{ih\cdot\theta}\,F(d\theta).$

Substitute the spectral representation from step 2.1 into each summand of step 1.3. Linearity permits moving the finite sum through the integral, and $\sum_{j,k\in\Lambda_n}e^{-i(j-k)\cdot(\lambda-\theta)} =\left|\sum_{j\in\Lambda_n}e^{-ij\cdot(\lambda-\theta)}\right|^2.$ After dividing by $(2\pi)^dn^d$ this is precisely $\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)] =\int_{\mathbb T^d}\Phi_n(\lambda-\theta)\,F(d\theta).$

The displayed kernel factors into nonnegative one-dimensional kernels. For each coordinate, expanding the finite square and applying angular orthogonality [F10] to each integer exponent $a-b$ gives $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac1{2\pi n} \left|\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}e^{-iax}\right|^2dx=1.$ The Countable Choice hypothesis of [F10] follows from AC by [F11] and [A1]. Fubini [F8] for the finite product then gives $\int_{\mathbb T^d}\Phi_n(x)\,dx=1,$ and nonnegativity follows from the squared modulus.

citations.quote:
Let $T\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, have its relative Borel sigma-algebra, and
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be one probability space. A **real random
field** indexed by $T$ is a family $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ of real random variables
$X(s):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on that space. This is coordinate measurability:
each map $(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ with $s$ fixed is measurable in
$\omega$. The field is **jointly measurable** when the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ from
$(T\times\Omega,\mathcal B(T)\otimes\mathcal F)$ to
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Joint measurability is an
additional hypothesis when a spatial Lebesgue integral is used; it is not part
of coordinate measurability.

Write $\mathcal L(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))$ for the pushforward law of a finite
coordinate tuple ([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). The field is **strictly stationary** on $T$ when, for every
finite tuple $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$ and every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ for which
$s_i+u\in T$ for all $i$, these joint laws are invariant under the common
translation $s_i\mapsto s_i+u$. This extends the integer-shift convention for
time series in [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] to spatial
indices.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs
of sites.

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its
mean is one constant $m$, and there is a function $C:T-T\to\mathbb R$ such
that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$
For a wide-stationary field on all of $\mathbb R^d$, it is **wide isotropic**
when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put
$\Delta_hX(s):=X(s+h)-X(s)$. The field is **intrinsically stationary of order
two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of
$\Delta_hX(s)$ are finite and independent of the admissible starting site
$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of
$\mathbb C$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]) and the multiplication of
$\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$,
$\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every Borel measure finite on compact sets on a second-countable LCH space is regular.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $(Y_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}$ be real square-integrable
random variables with constant mean $\mu$ and lag-dependent covariance
$$c(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{j+h},Y_j),$$
independent of $j$. Assume the Axiom of Choice and Dependent Choice. Then there
is a unique finite positive Radon measure $F$ on the angular torus $\mathbb T^d$
such that
$$c(h)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}e^{ih\cdot\theta}\,F(d\theta), \qquad h\in\mathbb Z^d.$$
For the periodogram $I_n$ of
[[def-regular-grid-periodogram-and-smoother]], define the product Fejer kernel
$$\Phi_n(x):=\frac1{(2\pi)^dn^d} \left|\sum_{j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}^d}e^{-ij\cdot x}\right|^2 =\prod_{r=1}^d\frac1{2\pi n} \left|\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}e^{-iax_r}\right|^2.$$
Then, for every $n\ge1$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb T^d$,
$$\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)] =\int_{\mathbb T^d}\Phi_n(\lambda-\theta)\,F(d\theta).$$
The kernel is nonnegative and has integral one with respect to product angular
Lebesgue measure. The spectral measure and density here belong to the
lattice-indexed observations on the dual torus.

On the set $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of pairs of natural numbers, define

$$(a,b) \sim (c,d) \iff a + d = b + c.$$

This is an equivalence relation ([[lem-int-equivalence]]). The **integers** are
the quotient

$$\mathbb{Z} := (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) / \sim,$$

and we write $[(a,b)]$ for the equivalence class of $(a,b)$.

The relation $(a,b) \sim (c,d) \iff a + d = b + c$ on
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-integers]]) is an equivalence relation.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $A$, let $A/{\sim}$ be its
quotient set and let $\pi := \{\,(a,C) \in A \times (A/{\sim}) : C = [a]\,\}$,
the quotient map. Let $f : A \to B$. Then $\pi$ is a surjective function
$A \to A/{\sim}$ with $\pi(a) = [a]$, and:

- (i) there is a function $g : A/{\sim} \to B$ with $g \circ \pi = f$ if and only if $f(a) = f(a')$ whenever $a \sim a'$;
- (ii) when such a $g$ exists it is unique, and it satisfies $g([a]) = f(a)$ for every $a \in A$.

$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the
plane of pairs of naturals is countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

The bijection is exhibited, not merely asserted to exist. Define $2^m$ by
recursion on $m$ ([[thm-recursion]]) by $2^0 = 1$ and $2^{\sigma(m)} = 2^m + 2^m$,
and set

$$J(m,n) = 2^m \cdot \sigma(n + n), \qquad \text{that is} \qquad J(m,n) = 2^m(2n+1).$$

Then $J$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, and $\sigma$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, so $\sigma^{-1} \circ J$ is a bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. What makes $J$ bijective is the
decomposition of a nonzero natural into a power of two times an odd number,
existence and uniqueness both.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.
If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from

excess $(W_n+K)\setminus W_n$ in the display is required to be Lebesgue

enlargement adds a negligible relative volume.

citations.quote:
A topological space $(X, \mathcal{T})$ ([[def-topological-space]]) is **locally
compact** when

> every point of $X$ has a compact neighbourhood:

that is, for every $x \in X$ there is a neighbourhood $N$ of $x$
([[def-neighbourhood-top]]) that is a compact subset of $X$
([[def-compact-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**A neighbourhood need not be open here**, and that is what makes the condition
the weak one it is meant to be: $N$ is required only to contain some open set
containing $x$. Writing "compact **open** neighbourhood" instead would define a
strictly stronger property, satisfied by no space in which a point has no compact
open neighbourhood, $\mathbb{R}$ among them; and requiring the compact set merely
to *contain* $x$ would define a property so weak that every space with a
singleton has it, singletons being compact.

**Every compact space is locally compact**, since $X$ itself is a neighbourhood
of each of its points and is a compact subset of itself. The converse fails, and
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is the standard witness.

**What the condition says in a metric space.** Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
carrying its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metrizable-space]]),
with balls as in [[def-metric-ball]], and let $x \in X$. Then

> $x$ has a compact neighbourhood **if and only if** there are a real $r > 0$ and
> a compact $K \subseteq X$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq K$.

*Both directions are immediate and are discharged here.* If $N$ is a compact
neighbourhood of $x$, fix an open $U$ with $x \in U \subseteq N$; by
[[def-metric-topology]] there is $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U \subseteq N$, so
$K := N$ serves. Conversely, if $B(x,r) \subseteq K$ with $K$ compact, then $K$
contains the open set $B(x,r)$, which contains $x$, so $K$ is a neighbourhood of
$x$ and is compact. Compactness of a subset of $(X,d)$ means the same thing read
metrically and read topologically
([[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]]), so the criterion may be
applied with either development's theorems.

**$\mathbb{R}^n$ is locally compact for every $n \ge 1$.** Give $\mathbb{R}^n$
the product topology, which is the metric topology of the Euclidean metric $d_2$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[cor-heine-borel-in-the-product-topology]]). For
$p \in \mathbb{R}^n$ the set

$$Q_p \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : d_2(x,p) \le 1 \,\}$$

is closed, being the complement of the union of the open balls $B(y, d_2(y,p) - 1)$
over the points $y$ with $d_2(y,p) > 1$, and it is bounded
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]), lying inside $B(p, 2)$; so $Q_p$ is compact by
[[cor-heine-borel-in-the-product-topology]]. It contains the open ball $B(p,1)$,
which contains $p$, so it is a compact neighbourhood of $p$. The space
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is not compact, so local compactness is strictly weaker than
compactness.

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). Then:

1. **A neighbourhood base of compact sets.** If $X$ is locally compact
   ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) and Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]), then
   every neighbourhood $N$ of a point $x \in X$ ([[def-neighbourhood-top]])
   contains a compact neighbourhood of $x$; so the compact neighbourhoods of $x$
   form a neighbourhood base at $x$.
2. **Heredity along open and closed subspaces.** If $X$ is locally compact and
   Hausdorff and $S \subseteq X$ is open, then the subspace $S$ is locally
   compact ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). If $X$ is locally compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed, then the subspace $F$ is locally compact; no
   Hausdorff hypothesis is used for this half.
3. **Shrinking inside an open set.** If $X$ is locally compact and Hausdorff,
   $O \subseteq X$ is open and $x \in O$, there is an open $V$ with
   $$x \in V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq O$$
   and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of $X$.
4. **Compact sets sit in open sets with compact closure.** If $X$ is locally
   compact and Hausdorff and $K \subseteq X$ is compact, there is an open
   $V \subseteq X$ with $K \subseteq V$ and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of
   $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**No choice principle is used**; every cover produced below is defined by a
formula and thinned by [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns
members rather than indices.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim: Fix an at most countable basis $\mathcal B$ for $S$ and let $\mathcal U=\{U\in\mathcal B:\overline U\text{ is compact}\}$. For any $x\in S$, [F2] with $O=S$ gives an open $V$ containing $x$ whose closure is compact. The basis property gives $U\in\mathcal B$ with $x\in U\subseteq V$; then $\overline U\subseteq\overline V$, and $\overline U$ is closed in the compact space $\overline V$, hence compact by [F3]. Thus $\mathcal U$ is an at most countable open cover of $S$.

If $S=\varnothing$, take $K_n=\varnothing$. Otherwise enumerate the subfamily $\mathcal U$ by filtering the fixed countable basis in its given enumeration; if the subfamily is finite, repeat its last member. Put $K_n=\bigcup_{j=1}^n\overline U_j$. An open cover of $K_n$ restricts to an open cover of each of the finitely many compact sets $\overline U_j$; taking the union of their finite subcovers gives a finite subcover of $K_n$. Thus $K_n$ is compact. The sequence is increasing, and its union is $S$ because $\mathcal U$ covers $S$.

Let $C\subseteq S$ be compact. The open cover $\mathcal U$ of $C$ has a finite subcover by the definition of compactness. Let $n$ be at least every index in that finite subcover. Then $C\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^nU_j\subseteq K_n$. Thus every compact $C$ is contained in some $K_n$.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 give the required increasing compact exhaustion and its cofinal containment property. The construction uses only a fixed countable basis and finite subcovers, so it invokes no choice principle.

citations.quote:
Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: The function $\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\zeta(B)]$ is defined for every Borel set $B$ by [F1] and [F2], and $\nu(\varnothing)=0$ because each measure $\zeta_\omega$ vanishes at $\varnothing$.

Let $f\ge0$ be Borel and choose $s_n\uparrow f$ as in [F4]. If $s_n$ is simple, its integral against $\zeta$ is a finite nonnegative linear combination of the measurable evaluations in [F1], hence is measurable. For each $\omega$, monotone convergence for the measure $\zeta_\omega$ gives $\zeta_\omega(s_n)\uparrow\zeta_\omega(f)$. The pointwise-limit result [F5] therefore makes $\omega\mapsto\zeta_\omega(f)$ measurable.

Let $(B_j)_{j\ge1}$ be pairwise disjoint Borel sets. For every $\omega$, $\zeta_\omega( igcup_jB_j)=\sum_j\zeta_\omega(B_j)$ by [F1] and [F6]. The finite partial sums increase, so [F3] gives $
u( igcup_jB_j)=\lim_n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbb E[\zeta(B_j)] =\sum_j
u(B_j)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves that $
u$ is a measure.

For a nonnegative simple $s=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j1_{B_j}$, the definition $
u(B)=\mathbb E[\zeta(B)]$ and finite linearity give $\mathbb E[\zeta(s)]=\int s\,d
u$. For the increasing sequence from step 1.2, both $\zeta(s_n)\uparrow\zeta(f)$ pathwise and $\int s_n\,d
u\uparrow\int f\,d
u$; applying [F3] to both nonnegative integrals proves the expectation identity.
For compact $K$, local finiteness of $\nu$ at $K$ means exactly $\nu(K)=\mathbb E[\zeta(K)]<\infty$ by its definition. Requiring this for all compact $K$ proves the final equivalence.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its

$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then
$\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
