An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Let $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ be a fixed finite family with $m\ge1$ in a statistical experiment, and let $p_i$ be a valid p-value for $H_{0i}$ as in [[def-null-valid-p-value-and-fwer-fdr]]. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, reject $H_{0i}$ exactly when $p_i(X)\le\alpha/m$. Then, for every $\theta$ in the parameter space,
$$P_\theta\{\text{at least one true null is rejected}\}=P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)\le\alpha.$$
The bound holds for every true-null configuration, including the global null and configurations with false nulls, and for arbitrary dependence among the p-values. This is strong FWER control; it is not an FDR guarantee.

A **p-value statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

A **statistic** with target measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

$$R=|\mathcal R|,\qquad V=|\mathcal R\cap I_0|.$$

The **false discovery proportion** is

$$\operatorname{FDP}:=\frac{V}{R\vee1},\qquad R\vee1:=\max(R,1),$$

and the **false discovery rate** is

$$\operatorname{FDR}:=\mathbb E_P\!\left[\frac{V}{R\vee1}\right].$$

The **family-wise error rate** is

$$\operatorname{FWER}:=P(V\ge1).$$

Since $V\le R$ whenever $R>0$ and $V=0$ when $R=0$, the FDP is a measurable
random variable in $[0,1]$ and its expectation is finite. These definitions
use the fixed true-null set for the specified law; they do not assert that FDR
and FWER are equal except in the global-null case.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: For $1\le r\le m-1$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, $\{y_{(r)}\le t\}$ is the finite union over $r$-element index sets $J$ of $\bigcap_{j\in J}\{y_j\le t\}$, since at least $r$ remaining values are at most $t$ exactly when the $r$th ordered value is at most $t$. Each coordinate cylinder is measurable in the stated finite product structure by [F1] and [F3], so these sublevel sets are Borel. Since the closed left rays generate $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ by [F4], each order statistic is Borel by [F2]. The coordinate-deletion projection from $[0,1]^m$ to $[0,1]^{m-1}$ is measurable: preimages of measurable rectangles are finite intersections of coordinate cylinders, and the rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra by [F3]. Thus lifting a Borel set in the remaining-coordinate space gives a Borel set in the full product. If $y\le z$ coordinatewise, at least $r$ coordinates of $z$ are at most $z_{(r)}$; their corresponding coordinates of $y$ are also at most $z_{(r)}$, so $y_{(r)}\le z_{(r)}$. Every remaining-coordinate order statistic is therefore coordinatewise nondecreasing.

Fix $k$ and suppose $p_i\le c_k$. Rank $k$ passes exactly when at least $k-1$ other coordinates are at most $c_k$, which is $y_{(k-1)}\le c_k$; for $k=1$ this holds by $y_{(0)}=0$. For each $j>k$, since $p_i\le c_k\le c_j$, rank $j$ passes exactly when at least $j-1$ other coordinates are at most $c_j$, namely $y_{(j-1)}\le c_j$. Hence $R=k$ exactly when the first condition of $C_{i,k}$ holds and every higher rank fails, which is $p_{-i}\in C_{i,k}$. In that case $i$ must be among the first $k$ ranks: otherwise $p_{(k+1)}\le p_i\le c_k\le c_{k+1}$ would make rank $k+1$ pass. Conversely, if $R=k$ and $i$ is rejected, then $p_i\le p_{(k)}\le c_k$, rank $k$ passes and every higher rank fails, so the conditions defining $C_{i,k}$ hold.

For any remaining vector $y$, replace coordinate $i$ by $0$. Since $c_1>0$, rank one passes, so the resulting rejection count is some $r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. By step 2.1, $y\in C_{i,r}$; hence the sets cover the space. If $k<\ell$ and $y\in C_{i,k}$, its condition at $r=\ell-1$ gives $y_{(\ell-1)}>c_\ell$, while membership in $C_{i,\ell}$ would give $y_{(\ell-1)}\le c_\ell$. Thus the sets are disjoint. They are Borel by step 1.1 and their finite defining inequalities.

If $y\in C_{i,j}$ for some $j\le k<m$, the defining inequalities include $y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}$ for every $r\ge k$, so $D_{i,k}$ is contained in the displayed intersection. Conversely, suppose those inequalities hold and set $p_i=0$. Rank one passes, but no rank $\ell\ge k+1$ can pass: that would require $y_{(\ell-1)}\le c_\ell$, contrary to the assumed condition at $r=\ell-1$. Thus the rejection count is some $j\le k$, and step 2.1 puts $y$ in $C_{i,j}$. This proves the formula; when $k=m$, step 3.1 gives $D_{i,m}$ equal to the whole space. The formula is a finite intersection of Borel order-statistic superlevel sets and is coordinatewise increasing by step 1.1.

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. $$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$

$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Input an integer $m\ge1$, observed values $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in[0,1]$ of p-value statistics ([[def-p-value]]), and a target level $q\in(0,1)$. Let $H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m1/j$ be the harmonic number from [[def-harmonic-number-for-set-cover-analysis]]. For $k=1,\ldots,m$, set

$$c_k:=\frac{kq}{mH_m}.$$

Order the pairs $(p_i,i)$ lexicographically, so equal values are ordered by their original indices, and write the ordered values $p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}$. Set

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le c_k\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$

Reject exactly the hypotheses at ranks $1,\ldots,R$; when $R=0$, reject none. Because $H_m\ge1$, each critical value satisfies $0<c_k\le q/H_m\le q<1$. This definition specifies the procedure; no FDR guarantee is asserted here.

Let $m\ge1$, $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\in[0,1]^m$, and critical values $0<c_1\le\cdots\le c_m\le1$. Give $[0,1]^m$ its finite product of the trace Borel sigma-algebras on $[0,1]$. Define the step-up rule by

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le c_k\}\cup\{0\}\bigr),$$

rejecting exactly ranks $1,\ldots,R$. Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Give the remaining-coordinate space $[0,1]^{m-1}$ its finite product of the trace Borel sigma-algebras, with the empty product on the singleton empty tuple when $m=1$. Write the remaining values in increasing order as $y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(m-1)}$, and set $y_{(0)}=0$. For $1\le k\le m$, let

$$C_{i,k}:=\{y_{(k-1)}\le c_k\}\cap\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$

with an empty intersection interpreted as the whole remaining-coordinate space. Put $D_{i,k}:=\bigcup_{j=1}^k C_{i,j}$. For $x\in[0,1]^m$, let $I_i(x)=1$ if the rule rejects coordinate $i$, and $I_i(x)=0$ otherwise. Then:

1. For every $k$, the following identity of subsets of $[0,1]^m$ holds:
   $$\{x\in[0,1]^m:I_i(x)=1,\ R(x)=k\}=\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_i\le c_k\}\cap\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_{-i}\in C_{i,k}\}.$$
   In particular, every input in the right-hand side has exactly $k$ rejections and rejects $i$.
2. The sets $C_{i,1},\ldots,C_{i,m}$ are a disjoint Borel partition of $[0,1]^{m-1}$.
3. For $k<m$,
   $$D_{i,k}=\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$
   and $D_{i,m}$ is the whole space. Each $D_{i,k}$ is a coordinatewise increasing Borel set.

For $m=1$, the remaining-coordinate space is the singleton empty tuple with its full sigma-algebra, and $C_{i,1}=D_{i,1}$ is the whole space.

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: The bounded FDP is a finite sum over true-null indices and the realized rejection count; indicator expectation and finite linearity turn it into the displayed probability sum.
For each true-null coordinate, the step-up rejection partition and intervals J_j yield a weighted interval sum bounded by sum_j P(p_i∈J_j)/j.
The finite CDF differences telescope by summation by parts; superuniformity F_j≤jt gives the bound tH_m=q/m, including the zero endpoint.
Combining the per-null q/m bound with the finite true-null sum gives FDR≤(m_0/m)q≤q, with an empty outer sum when m_0=0.

boundaries.evidence: If there are no true nulls, the outer sum in step 1.1 is empty and step 3.1 gives FDR=0.
Validity at u=0 gives P(p_i=0)=0; step 1.2 removes that null event and step 2.1 sets F_0=0.
For m=1, H_1=1 and there is one interval; step 2.1 gives tH_1=q, equal to q/m.
The interval masses need not be bounded by their widths for discrete valid p-values; step 2.1 instead uses only F_j≤jt and finite summation by parts.
The level is q∈(0,1), mt=q/H_m<1, and validity is applied at all cutoffs jt including zero in steps 1.2–3.1.
Steps 1.1–4.1 use finite sums, a deterministic partition, and finite summation by parts; no choice principle or dependence assumption is used.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $m\ge1$, and let $\mathbf P=(P_1,\ldots,P_m):\Omega\to[0,1]^m$ be a random vector whose coordinates are p-value statistics ([[def-p-value]]). Fix a designated true-null index set $I_0\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$. For $i\in I_0$, write $\mu_i$ for the law of $P_i$ under $\mathbb P$ and define its support relative to $[0,1]$ by

$$\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i):=\{x\in[0,1]:\mu_i(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}.$$

Give each coordinate $[0,1]$ its trace Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and give $[0,1]^m$ the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). In this definition, “Borel set” means a member of that product sigma-algebra; thus “increasing measurable set” means coordinatewise increasing in this stated structure. The unit-interval lemma proves that $[0,1]$ with this trace Borel structure is standard Borel ([[lem-unit-interval-is-standard-borel]]). The finite-product result then makes $[0,1]^m$ with the specified product sigma-algebra a standard-Borel target ([[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]); its finite-product proof uses only finite choice in ZF. Under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), this target has a regular conditional distribution given $\sigma(P_i)$, and the conditional-law factorization result supplies a kernel $K_i:[0,1]\to[0,1]^m$ representing the conditional law of $\mathbf P$ given $P_i=x$ ([[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]], [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]], [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]).

The law of $\mathbf P$ is **positive regression dependent on the true-null coordinates (PRDS on $I_0$)** if, for each $i\in I_0$, such a conditional-law version can be chosen so that for every coordinatewise increasing Borel set $D$, the function

$$x\longmapsto K_i(x,D)$$

is nondecreasing on $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)$. If $I_0=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous. The monotonicity condition is a full conditional-law requirement; pairwise correlations alone do not verify it.

Let $m\ge1$, $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\in[0,1]^m$, and critical values $0<c_1\le\cdots\le c_m\le1$. Give $[0,1]^m$ its finite product of the trace Borel sigma-algebras on $[0,1]$. Define the step-up rule by

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le c_k\}\cup\{0\}\bigr),$$

rejecting exactly ranks $1,\ldots,R$. Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Give the remaining-coordinate space $[0,1]^{m-1}$ its finite product of the trace Borel sigma-algebras, with the empty product on the singleton empty tuple when $m=1$. Write the remaining values in increasing order as $y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(m-1)}$, and set $y_{(0)}=0$. For $1\le k\le m$, let

$$C_{i,k}:=\{y_{(k-1)}\le c_k\}\cap\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$

with an empty intersection interpreted as the whole remaining-coordinate space. Put $D_{i,k}:=\bigcup_{j=1}^k C_{i,j}$. For $x\in[0,1]^m$, let $I_i(x)=1$ if the rule rejects coordinate $i$, and $I_i(x)=0$ otherwise. Then:

1. For every $k$, the following identity of subsets of $[0,1]^m$ holds:
   $$\{x\in[0,1]^m:I_i(x)=1,\ R(x)=k\}=\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_i\le c_k\}\cap\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_{-i}\in C_{i,k}\}.$$
   In particular, every input in the right-hand side has exactly $k$ rejections and rejects $i$.
2. The sets $C_{i,1},\ldots,C_{i,m}$ are a disjoint Borel partition of $[0,1]^{m-1}$.
3. For $k<m$,
   $$D_{i,k}=\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$
   and $D_{i,m}$ is the whole space. Each $D_{i,k}$ is a coordinatewise increasing Borel set.

For $m=1$, the remaining-coordinate space is the singleton empty tuple with its full sigma-algebra, and $C_{i,1}=D_{i,1}$ is the whole space.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $m\ge1$, and let $\mathbf P=(P_1,\ldots,P_m):\Omega\to[0,1]^m$ be a random vector whose coordinates are p-value statistics ([[def-p-value]]). Fix a designated true-null index set $I_0\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$. For $i\in I_0$, write $\mu_i$ for the law of $P_i$ under $\mathbb P$ and define its support relative to $[0,1]$ by

$$\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i):=\{x\in[0,1]:\mu_i(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}.$$

Give each coordinate $[0,1]$ its trace Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and give $[0,1]^m$ the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). In this definition, “Borel set” means a member of that product sigma-algebra; thus “increasing measurable set” means coordinatewise increasing in this stated structure. The unit-interval lemma proves that $[0,1]$ with this trace Borel structure is standard Borel ([[lem-unit-interval-is-standard-borel]]). The finite-product result then makes $[0,1]^m$ with the specified product sigma-algebra a standard-Borel target ([[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]); its finite-product proof uses only finite choice in ZF. Under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), this target has a regular conditional distribution given $\sigma(P_i)$, and the conditional-law factorization result supplies a kernel $K_i:[0,1]\to[0,1]^m$ representing the conditional law of $\mathbf P$ given $P_i=x$ ([[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]], [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]], [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]).

The law of $\mathbf P$ is **positive regression dependent on the true-null coordinates (PRDS on $I_0$)** if, for each $i\in I_0$, such a conditional-law version can be chosen so that for every coordinatewise increasing Borel set $D$, the function

$$x\longmapsto K_i(x,D)$$

is nondecreasing on $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)$. If $I_0=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous. The monotonicity condition is a full conditional-law requirement; pairwise correlations alone do not verify it.

derivations.claim: Put $c_k=kq/m$, $A_k:=\{P_i\le c_k\}$, and $B_{i,k}:=\{P_{-i}\in C_{i,k}\}$. If $P(A_k)>0$, set $a_k:=P(A_k\cap B_{i,k})/P(A_k)$; otherwise set $a_k=0$. By [F2], $I_i/(R\vee1)=\sum_{k=1}^m k^{-1}\mathbf1_{A_k\cap B_{i,k}}$. The terms are bounded and the sum is finite, so [F5]–[F7] give $\mathbb E[I_i/(R\vee1)]=\sum_{k=1}^m(P(A_k)/k)a_k$; a zero-probability $A_k$ contributes zero by the definition of $a_k$.

For each $k$, lift $D_{i,k}$ to $\widetilde D_{i,k}:=\{p\in[0,1]^m:p_{-i}\in D_{i,k}\}$. The coordinate-deletion map from $[0,1]^m$ to the remaining-coordinate product is measurable: the preimage of each measurable rectangle is a finite intersection of coordinate cylinders, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Hence $\widetilde D_{i,k}$ is Borel, and it is coordinatewise increasing. Let $g_k(x):=K_i(x,\widetilde D_{i,k})$, nondecreasing on the support by [F1] and [A1]; the kernel exists on this standard-Borel interface under [A2].

Write $S_i=\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)$. The family $\mathcal U:=\{(a,b)\cap[0,1]:a,b\in\mathbb Q,\ a<b\}$ is a basis for the relative topology on $[0,1]$. If $U$ is relative open and $x\in U$, write $U=O\cap[0,1]$ with $O$ open in $\mathbb R$ by [F8]; choose $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq O$ using [F8], then use rational density from [F8] to choose $a,b\in\mathbb Q$ with $x-\varepsilon<a<x<b<x+\varepsilon$. Thus $x\in(a,b)\cap[0,1]\subseteq U$. Since $\mathbb Q\times\mathbb Q$ is nonempty and at most countable by [F8], [F9] gives an enumeration $((a_n,b_n))_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of it, whose interval images enumerate $\mathcal U$; hence the basis is countable. Let $E_n=(a_n,b_n)\cap[0,1]$ if $a_n<b_n$ and $\mu_i((a_n,b_n)\cap[0,1])=0$, and $E_n=\varnothing$ otherwise. By the definition of support in [[def-prds-on-true-null-coordinates]],
   $$[0,1]\setminus S_i=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n.$$
   Indeed, a point outside the support has a relative open null neighborhood and hence a basis neighborhood contained in it, which occurs in the enumeration; conversely, membership in any such null basis neighborhood excludes support membership. The right-hand side is a countable union of null Borel sets, so [F8] gives $\mu_i([0,1]\setminus S_i)=0$. Thus $S_i$ is Borel and $\mu_i(S_i)=1$.

By [F4], whenever $P(A_k)>0$,
   $$\frac{P(A_k\cap\{P_{-i}\in D_{i,k}\})}{P(A_k)}=\frac{\int_{[0,c_k]}g_k(x)\,\mu_i(dx)}{\mu_i([0,c_k])}.$$
   For fixed $k<m$, this average is at most the corresponding average over $[0,c_{k+1}]$. By step 1.3, both averages may be restricted to $S_i$ without changing them. Every supported $x\le c_k$ is below every supported $y\in(c_k,c_{k+1}]$, so $g_k(x)\le g_k(y)$ by [F1] and [A1]. The larger-cutoff average is a mixture of the first average and the average over the added interval; the latter is at least the first whenever it has positive mass, and if it has zero mass the two averages agree.
By [F3], $P(A_k)\le c_k=kq/m$ for every $k$. Substituting into step 1.1 yields $\mathbb E[I_i/(R\vee1)]\le(q/m)\sum_{k=1}^m a_k$.

Let $k_0$ be the first index with $P(A_{k_0})>0$, if one exists; then $a_j=0$ for $j<k_0$, and $C_{i,k_0}\subseteq D_{i,k_0}$ gives $a_{k_0}\le P(P_{-i}\in D_{i,k_0}\mid A_{k_0})\le1$ by step 1.4. For $k>k_0$, suppose $\sum_{j<k}a_j\le P(P_{-i}\in D_{i,k-1}\mid A_{k-1})$. Since $P(A_{k-1})>0$ and $A_{k-1}\subseteq A_k$, step 1.4 applied to the nondecreasing $g_{k-1}$ makes this at most $P(P_{-i}\in D_{i,k-1}\mid A_k)$. Also $P(A_k)>0$, so [F4] gives $a_k=P(P_{-i}\in C_{i,k}\mid A_k)$. The disjoint union $D_{i,k}=D_{i,k-1}\,\dot\cup\,C_{i,k}$ from [F2] then yields $\sum_{j\le k}a_j\le P(P_{-i}\in D_{i,k}\mid A_k)$, completing the induction.

If $k_0$ exists, step 2.2 at $k=m$ and $D_{i,m}$ equal to the whole space give $\sum_{k=1}^ma_k\le1$. If no such $k_0$ exists, all $P(A_k)=0$ and every $a_k=0$, so the same bound holds. Substituting into step 2.1 proves the contribution inequality.

citations.quote:
An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $m\ge1$, and let $\mathbf P=(P_1,\ldots,P_m):\Omega\to[0,1]^m$ be a random vector whose coordinates are p-value statistics ([[def-p-value]]). Fix a designated true-null index set $I_0\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$. For $i\in I_0$, write $\mu_i$ for the law of $P_i$ under $\mathbb P$ and define its support relative to $[0,1]$ by

$$\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i):=\{x\in[0,1]:\mu_i(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}.$$

Give each coordinate $[0,1]$ its trace Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and give $[0,1]^m$ the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). In this definition, “Borel set” means a member of that product sigma-algebra; thus “increasing measurable set” means coordinatewise increasing in this stated structure. The unit-interval lemma proves that $[0,1]$ with this trace Borel structure is standard Borel ([[lem-unit-interval-is-standard-borel]]). The finite-product result then makes $[0,1]^m$ with the specified product sigma-algebra a standard-Borel target ([[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]); its finite-product proof uses only finite choice in ZF. Under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), this target has a regular conditional distribution given $\sigma(P_i)$, and the conditional-law factorization result supplies a kernel $K_i:[0,1]\to[0,1]^m$ representing the conditional law of $\mathbf P$ given $P_i=x$ ([[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]], [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]], [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]).

The law of $\mathbf P$ is **positive regression dependent on the true-null coordinates (PRDS on $I_0$)** if, for each $i\in I_0$, such a conditional-law version can be chosen so that for every coordinatewise increasing Borel set $D$, the function

$$x\longmapsto K_i(x,D)$$

is nondecreasing on $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)$. If $I_0=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous. The monotonicity condition is a full conditional-law requirement; pairwise correlations alone do not verify it.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Input $m\ge1$ p-values $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in[0,1]$ and a level $q\in(0,1)$.
Order the hypotheses by the keys $(p_i,i)$, so equal p-values are ordered by
their original index, and write the ordered values as
$p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}$. Set

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le kq/m\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$

Reject exactly the hypotheses at ranks $1,\ldots,R$. If the set in the
maximum is empty, then $R=0$ and no hypothesis is rejected. This is a
deterministic step-up rule for the supplied p-values; its FDR guarantee is a
separate theorem.

Input an integer $m\ge1$, observed values $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in[0,1]$ of p-value statistics ([[def-p-value]]), and a target level $q\in(0,1)$. Let $H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m1/j$ be the harmonic number from [[def-harmonic-number-for-set-cover-analysis]]. For $k=1,\ldots,m$, set

$$c_k:=\frac{kq}{mH_m}.$$

Order the pairs $(p_i,i)$ lexicographically, so equal values are ordered by their original indices, and write the ordered values $p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}$. Set

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le c_k\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$

Reject exactly the hypotheses at ranks $1,\ldots,R$; when $R=0$, reject none. Because $H_m\ge1$, each critical value satisfies $0<c_k\le q/H_m\le q<1$. This definition specifies the procedure; no FDR guarantee is asserted here.

For each integer $n\ge 1$ the $n$-th **harmonic number** is the finite sum
$$H_n:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{j},$$
taken over the finite index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ in the rational numbers. For the
empty index set one sets $H_0:=0$, the empty-sum convention. Thus
$H_1=1$, $H_2=3/2$, $H_3=11/6$ and so on, and each $H_n$ is a rational number
determined by the displayed finite recursion on the upper index. These are the
only harmonic values used in the set-cover analysis of this page.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let $m\ge1$, and fix a finite family of null hypotheses $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$. For each $i$, let $p_i$ be a p-value statistic valid for $H_{0i}$ in the sense of [[def-null-valid-p-value-and-fwer-fdr]]. For $\theta\in\Theta$, put

$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\theta\in H_{0i}\},\qquad m_0(\theta):=|I_0(\theta)|.$$

For every $q\in(0,1)$, the BY procedure in [[alg-benjamini-yekutieli-step-up-procedure]] satisfies

$$\operatorname{FDR}_\theta\le\frac{m_0(\theta)}{m}q\le q.$$

No dependence condition on the joint law of the p-values is required.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment, let $m\ge1$, and fix a finite family of null hypotheses $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with p-value statistics $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ valid for their respective nulls. For each $\theta$, write

$$I_0(\theta):=\{i:\theta\in H_{0i}\},\qquad m_0(\theta):=|I_0(\theta)|.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required for the regular conditional-law interface in [[def-prds-on-true-null-coordinates]]. Suppose that, under every $P_\theta$, the p-value vector $(p_1(X),\ldots,p_m(X))$ is PRDS on $I_0(\theta)$. Then for every $q\in(0,1)$, the ordinary BH procedure in [[alg-benjamini-hochberg-step-up-procedure]] satisfies

$$\operatorname{FDR}_\theta\le\frac{m_0(\theta)}m q\le q.$$

The PRDS assumption is imposed only on the true-null coordinates; no independence assumption is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The five masses sum to one, and the sum of the product point masses on $S^4$ is $(\sum_{s\in S}\mu(\{s\}))^4=1$, so these masses define a probability law on the finite sample space. For any subsets $B_1,\ldots,B_4\subseteq S$, summing the product masses over $B_1\times\cdots\times B_4$ factors as $\prod_i\mu(B_i)$; thus the coordinate p-values are mutually independent. Each coordinate has support $1/100,1/25,13/100,29/100,1$ and cumulative probabilities $1/100,4/100,13/100,29/100,1$, respectively. At each support value the cumulative probability equals that value; between successive support values it stays at the preceding value, and below $1/100$ it is zero. Thus $P(p_i\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$, so all four p-values are valid by [F2].

Fix a coordinate $i$. For $x\in S$, define $K_i(x,\cdot)$ as the law of the four-vector obtained by fixing coordinate $i$ at $x$ and drawing the other three coordinates independently from the specified marginal; for $x\notin S$, use a fixed point mass. Since $S$ is finite, each evaluation is Borel measurable and each section is a probability measure. For Borel $A\subseteq[0,1]$ and $D\subseteq[0,1]^4$, product-mass factorization gives $\int_A K_i(x,D)\,P_{p_i}(dx)=P(p_i\in A,\ p\in D)$, so this is a conditional law by [F4]. If $D$ is coordinatewise increasing and $x\le x'$ in $S$, then fixing any same remaining triple makes the vector at $x$ coordinatewise at most the vector at $x'$, so its indicator of $D$ is no larger. Averaging over the same three-coordinate product law yields $K_i(x,D)\le K_i(x',D)$. This holds for every $i$, and [F3] gives PRDS on the all-true-null set.

The event that the four coordinates take the four distinct values $1/100,1/25,13/100,29/100$ in any order has probability $4!(1/100)(3/100)(9/100)(16/100)>0$. On this event $H_4=25/12$. BH's critical values are $1/20,1/10,3/20,1/5$, so the first three ordered p-values pass and the fourth does not, giving $R_{BH}=3$. BY's critical values are $3/125,6/125,9/125,12/125$, so ranks one and two pass and rank three does not, giving $R_{BY}=2$.

For a candidate contrast value $\vartheta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\Delta_\vartheta(z)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{U(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{L(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right).$$
When $G(z)$ holds, $L(z)<U(z)$, and $\Delta_\vartheta(z)>0$, define
$$q_\vartheta(t,z)=\frac{\Phi((t-\vartheta)/s)-\Phi((L(z)-\vartheta)/s)}{\Delta_\vartheta(z)}\qquad (L(z)\le t\le U(z)).$$
For a total statistic on $\mathbb R^n$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=0$ when $y\notin S$ or when the denominator is zero; on the remaining part of $S$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=q_\vartheta(T(y),Z(y))$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selective-normal-pivot]], with $P_\mu(S)>0$. For $P_\mu(Z\in\cdot\mid S)$-almost every $z$, the conditional law of $T$ given $Z=z$ and $S$ is the $N(\theta,s^2)$ law restricted to $[L(z),U(z)]$ and normalized by $\Delta_\theta(z)>0$. Its CDF on that interval is $q_\theta(t,z)$. The pivot is Borel measurable on the selected data space. Consequently $q_\theta(Y)$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $(Z,S)$ wherever the normalizer is positive, and is also Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $S$ alone. The event $S$ is a single fixed polyhedron; no union-of-polyhedra claim is made.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal Y,\mathcal G),\mathcal M,(Q_\mu)_{\mu\in\mathcal M})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let $\tau:\mathcal M\to\Lambda$ be a parameter functional. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, a set-valued procedure $C:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal P(\Lambda)$ is a selective confidence set with coverage at least $1-\alpha$ if, for every $\mu\in\mathcal M$, its membership section $\{y:\tau(\mu)\in C(y)\}$ belongs to $\mathcal G$ and
$$Q_\mu\{y:\tau(\mu)\in C(y)\}\ge1-\alpha.$$
It is exact if equality holds for every $\mu$. Here the laws $Q_\mu$ are the laws after conditioning on the specified selection event. This is the membership-section coverage condition of [[def-confidence-set-and-coverage]] for an estimand $\tau(\mu)$; no measurable structure on $\mathcal M$ or $\Lambda$ is imposed.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a parameter-indexed family of measurable
real-valued quantities with a common sampling law. The maps $q_\theta$
may depend on the unknown parameter. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$
If $\nu(B)\ge1-\alpha$, then $C$ is a confidence set with coverage at
least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

derivations.claim: For any $\mu$ in the conditional experiment, [F1] gives $q_{\eta^T\mu}(Y)\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$ under $Q_\mu$. For $0\le u\le1$, the event $2\min\{q,1-q\}\le u$ is the union of the two tails $q\le u/2$ and $q\ge1-u/2$, whose uniform probabilities sum to $u$ (their intersection has measure zero). Hence $p_\vartheta$ is uniform under every $\mu\in H_0(\vartheta)$ and is measurable by the pivot formula; [F2] makes it a valid p-value.

If the alternative is nonempty, [F3] applied to $p_\vartheta$ gives conditional size at most $\alpha$. By [F4] size is the supremum of these null rejection probabilities; since every null law has the exact uniform p-value distribution from step 1.1, $Q_\mu(p_\vartheta\le\alpha)=\alpha$ for every null $\mu$, so the size is exactly $\alpha$.

By [F1], [F6], and [F8], $q_\mu(Y):=q_{\eta^T\mu}(Y)$ is a pivot in the conditional experiment. Its full-parameter inversion is $C_{\rm full}(Y)=\{\mu'\in\Theta_S:q_{\eta^T\mu'}(Y)\in[\alpha/2,1-\alpha/2]\}$. The acceptance interval has uniform probability $1-\alpha$, so [F7] gives exact coverage for $C_{\rm full}$. Its image under $\mu'\mapsto\eta^T\mu'$ is exactly $C_\eta(Y)$ by the definition of $\Theta_\eta$. For each fixed true $\mu$, membership $\eta^T\mu\in C_\eta(Y)$ is precisely $\alpha/2\le q_{\eta^T\mu}(Y)\le1-\alpha/2$, which has $Q_\mu$-probability $1-\alpha$ by [F1]. The membership section is measurable by the Borel pivot formula, so [F5] applies.

At alpha=1, the threshold test rejects with probability one and the central acceptance interval has uniform probability zero; steps 2.1 and 3.1 include alpha=1.

AC is inherited through the Gaussian pivot theorem and appears in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1; no additional witness selection is used.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix integers $n\ge1$ and $m\ge0$, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, a vector $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and a fixed nonzero vector $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$. Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise. Define the projection matrix and contrast direction
$$P_\eta=\frac{\eta\eta^T}{\|\eta\|^2},\qquad c_\eta=\frac{\eta}{\|\eta\|^2}.$$
The matrix $P_\eta$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{\eta\}$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]). For a vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, put
$$T(y)=\eta^Ty,\qquad Z(y)=(I_n-P_\eta)y.$$
Then $y=c_\eta T(y)+Z(y)$ and $\eta^TZ(y)=0$.

For row $j$ of $A$, written $a_j^T$, define
$$r_j=a_j^Tc_\eta,\qquad d_j(z)=b_j-a_j^Tz.$$
Let $J_-=\{j:r_j<0\}$, $J_+=\{j:r_j>0\}$, and $J_0=\{j:r_j=0\}$. Define
$$L(z)=\begin{cases}\max_{j\in J_-}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_-\ne\varnothing,\\-\infty,&J_-=\varnothing,\end{cases}\qquad U(z)=\begin{cases}\min_{j\in J_+}d_j(z)/r_j,&J_+\ne\varnothing,\\+\infty,&J_+=\varnothing.\end{cases}$$
Define $G(z)$ to hold exactly when $d_j(z)\ge0$ for every $j\in J_0$. The selection event is $S=\{y:Ay\le b\}$. The interval associated with $z$ is $I(z)=\varnothing$ if $G(z)$ fails or $L(z)>U(z)$, and is $[L(z),U(z)]$ otherwise. The next lemma proves that this interval describes precisely the fiber of $S$ along the contrast direction.

Assume AC. In the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selection-event-and-contrast-interval]], let $Y\sim N_n(\mu,\sigma^2I_n)$, where $\sigma>0$ is known ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]). Put $\theta=\eta^T\mu$, $s=\sigma\|\eta\|$, and let $\Phi$ be the standard normal CDF from [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]. Extend it by $\Phi(-\infty)=0$ and $\Phi(+\infty)=1$. For a candidate contrast value $\vartheta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\Delta_\vartheta(z)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{U(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{L(z)-\vartheta}{s}\right).$$
When $G(z)$ holds, $L(z)<U(z)$, and $\Delta_\vartheta(z)>0$, define
$$q_\vartheta(t,z)=\frac{\Phi((t-\vartheta)/s)-\Phi((L(z)-\vartheta)/s)}{\Delta_\vartheta(z)}\qquad (L(z)\le t\le U(z)).$$
For a total statistic on $\mathbb R^n$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=0$ when $y\notin S$ or when the denominator is zero; on the remaining part of $S$, set $q_\vartheta(y)=q_\vartheta(T(y),Z(y))$. The value assigned on zero-normalizer fibers is only a measurable extension; the conditional law given selection will give those fibers probability zero.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selective-normal-pivot]], with $P_\mu(S)>0$. For $P_\mu(Z\in\cdot\mid S)$-almost every $z$, the conditional law of $T$ given $Z=z$ and $S$ is the $N(\theta,s^2)$ law restricted to $[L(z),U(z)]$ and normalized by $\Delta_\theta(z)>0$. Its CDF on that interval is $q_\theta(t,z)$. The pivot is Borel measurable on the selected data space. Consequently $q_\theta(Y)$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $(Z,S)$ wherever the normalizer is positive, and is also Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on $S$ alone. The event $S$ is a single fixed polyhedron; no union-of-polyhedra claim is made.

Assume AC and the setup of [[def-polyhedral-selective-normal-pivot]], and suppose $P_\mu(S)>0$ for at least one $\mu\in\mathbb R^n$. Write $\Theta_S=\{\mu\in\mathbb R^n:P_\mu(S)>0\}$. The selected sample space is $S$ with trace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(S)=\{S\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\}$, and for $\mu\in\Theta_S$ let $Q_\mu=P_\mu(\,\cdot\mid S)$ be the conditional sampling law. For $\vartheta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$p_\vartheta(Y)=2\min\{q_\vartheta(Y),1-q_\vartheta(Y)\}.$$
For the point null $H_0(\vartheta)=\{\mu\in\Theta_S:\eta^T\mu=\vartheta\}$, if this null is nonempty then $p_\vartheta$ is a valid p-value in the conditional experiment $(Q_\mu)$ and is Uniform$(0,1)$ under every null law. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, rejecting when $p_\vartheta\le\alpha$ has conditional type-I error exactly $\alpha$; for any nonempty alternative $\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta_S\setminus H_0(\vartheta)$, it has size $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$.

For $0\le\alpha\le1$, put $\Theta_\eta=\{\eta^T\mu:\mu\in\Theta_S\}$ and
$$C_\eta(Y)=\{\vartheta\in\Theta_\eta:\alpha/2\le q_\vartheta(Y)\le1-\alpha/2\}.$$
This is an exact selective confidence set for the functional $\tau(\mu)=\eta^T\mu$ in the sense of [[def-exact-selective-confidence-set-for-a-functional]]: for every $\mu$ with $P_\mu(S)>0$,
$$Q_\mu\{\eta^T\mu\in C_\eta(Y)\}=1-\alpha.$$
The guarantee is for one fixed contrast and one fixed selection event, not simultaneous coverage over a selected family.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: The model is the isotropic Gaussian construction in [F8]; [F5] gives each scalar marginal as an affine image of a standard normal. For $\sigma>0$, [F6] gives $P_\mu(1<Y_1\le2)=\Phi((2-\mu_1)/\sigma)-\Phi((1-\mu_1)/\sigma)>0$ and $P_\mu(0<Y_2\le1)=\Phi((1-\mu_2)/\sigma)-\Phi((0-\mu_2)/\sigma)>0$. By [F7], the rectangle $(1,2]\times(0,1]$ has probability equal to the product of these positive probabilities; it lies in $S$, so $P_\mu(S)>0$. Here $c_\eta=(1,0)^T$. The single row has $r_1=(-1,1)c_\eta=-1$ and, at $z=(0,Y_2)$, $d_1(z)=-Y_2$. Thus $L(z)=d_1(z)/r_1=Y_2$, there are no upper constraints so $U(z)=+\infty$, and $G(z)$ is true. The event is exactly $Y_1\ge Y_2$, giving interval $[Y_2,+\infty)$.

Since $T=Y_1$, $\theta=\mu_1$, and $s=\sigma$, the definition [F2] gives $q_{\vartheta}(Y_1,Y_2)=[\Phi((Y_1-\vartheta)/\sigma)-\Phi((Y_2-\vartheta)/\sigma)]/[1-\Phi((Y_2-\vartheta)/\sigma)]$. At $(Y_1,Y_2)=(1,0)$, $\sigma=1$, and $\vartheta=0$, this becomes the displayed $q_0$.

Under the point null $\mu_1=0$, [F3] makes $q_0$ Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on selection, so [F4] gives the stated two-sided p-value and exact selective test. For general $\vartheta$, the set retaining $\alpha/2\le q_\vartheta\le1-\alpha/2$ has conditional coverage $1-\alpha$ by [F4]. No claim about a selected-family simultaneous guarantee is used.
