citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. A subset of
$X \times Y$ is a **measurable rectangle** if it has the form $A \times B$ with
$A \in \mathcal A$ and $B \in \mathcal B$.

The ambient sigma-algebras matter: the same set may be a measurable rectangle
for one pair $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)$ and not for another.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then
$\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

On a filtered probability space [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]], a **real stochastic process** is a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ of real random variables [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] on the same space. It is **adapted** when $X_n^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$ and every real Borel set $B$. It is **integrable** when $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, using [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

An integrable adapted process satisfies both conditions at each fixed time. Integrability here does not mean $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$: the deterministic process $X_n=n$ has $E|X_n|=n<\infty$ at every time but unbounded supremum. Measurability and finiteness of each integral are separate requirements. No versions, limits or choices are selected.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.
Assume AC. For every real integrable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and every sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, a conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ exists.
If $Y,Z$ are conditional-expectation versions of the same real integrable $X$ given $\mathcal G$, then $Y=Z$ almost surely.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. An integrable adapted real process $X$ [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]] is a **martingale**, **submartingale**, or **supermartingale** when, respectively, for every $n\ge0$,
$$E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le X_n\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
These are three separate conditions, with the convention that a submartingale has conditional future mean at least its present value. The conditional expectations are the almost-sure classes of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; that supplier inherits AC from its Radon–Nikodym existence proof. The definition itself selects no representative and assumes no completed filtration.

The condition is imposed at each adjacent pair of times. An all-pairs formulation requires a proof. No boundedness or independence is part of this definition, and no trivial or deterministic initial value is imposed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0})$ be a discrete filtration
on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$, it is adapted and integrable under $P$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws on a common
discrete filtered measurable space and let $E=(E_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nonnegative
test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$
[[def-nonnegative-test-supermartingale]]. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and
every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$$P\!\left(\sup_{t\ge0}E_t\ge\frac1\alpha\right)\le\alpha.$$

For a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$, a map
$$\tau:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$$
is a **stopping time** if $\{\tau\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\ge0$. It is **bounded** if some deterministic $N$ satisfies $\tau\le N$ almost surely, and **finite** if $P(\tau<\infty)=1$. These notions are distinct: finite does not mean bounded.

The event condition is literal, not merely modulo null sets; no completion of the filtration is assumed. Measurability as an extended-integer-valued random variable follows from the equivalent event tests below.

derivations.claim: Each $L_t$ is nonnegative by [F3] and $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by [F2] and [F5]. Applying [F4] with $g=1$ gives $\mathbb E_{P_0}L_t=P_1(\Omega)=1$ for every $t$, so each $L_t$ is integrable.

Thus $R$ is a nonnegative $P_1$-martingale by [F9].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

Assume AC. Let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on a common measurable space and let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be random elements of $(S,\Sigma)$ that are IID under each $P_j$, with one-coordinate law $Q_j$. Suppose $Q_1\ll Q_0$, let $\lambda=dQ_1/dQ_0$ be a nonnegative representative, and put $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_t)$. For every $t\ge1$,
$$L_t:=\prod_{i=1}^t\lambda(X_i)$$
is a version of $d(P_1|_{\mathcal F_t})/d(P_0|_{\mathcal F_t})$.

Assume the [[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]], which states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0})$ be a discrete filtration on a common measurable space and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on it. Assume that for every $t\ge0$, the restrictions $P_0|_{\mathcal F_t}$ and $P_1|_{\mathcal F_t}$ are mutually absolutely continuous: each restriction assigns measure zero to exactly the same $\mathcal F_t$ events as the other. For each $t$, choose a nonnegative $\mathcal F_t$-measurable representative $L_t$ of the likelihood-ratio density $d(P_1|_{\mathcal F_t})/d(P_0|_{\mathcal F_t})$ [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]]. The filtration and stopping-time conventions are those of [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]] and [[def-discrete-stopping-time]].

Input thresholds $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)$. At times $t=1,2,\ldots$, compute $L_t$ and apply these instructions:

1. If $L_t\ge1/\alpha$, stop and decide $H_1$.
2. Otherwise, if $L_t\le\beta$, stop and decide $H_0$.
3. Otherwise continue to the next observation.

The two boundaries are disjoint because $\beta<1<1/\alpha$. The output time is
$$\tau=\inf\{t\ge1:L_t\ge1/\alpha\text{ or }L_t\le\beta\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=\infty.$$
If $\tau=\infty$, the procedure has no finite terminal decision. It does not itself assert that a crossing occurs.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

derivations.claim: Let $r$ be any nonnegative RN representative of $Q_1$ with respect to $Q_0$. Since $\int r\,dQ_0=1$, the set where $r=\infty$ is $Q_0$-null and hence $Q_1$-null. On $A=\{r=0\}$ the change-of-measure identity [F5] gives $Q_1(A)=\int_A r\,dQ_0=0$; equivalence $Q_0\ll Q_1$ then makes $A$ $Q_0$-null too. Replacing $r$ by $1$ on these common null sets yields a finite strictly positive measurable representative $\lambda$ of the same density class. Its range lies in $(0,\infty)$, so it is measurable into that subspace with its Borel sigma-algebra $\{B\cap(0,\infty):B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$. Although the logarithm is continuous on this subspace, [F8] only covers Euclidean domains. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\log^{-1}(U)$ is open in $(0,\infty)$ and therefore Borel there; since open sets generate $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is Borel measurable. Thus [F9] makes $Z=\log\circ\lambda$ real-valued and measurable.

For each $j$, the variables $Z_i:=Z(X_i)$ are IID under $P_j$: measurability gives the same pushforward law for all coordinates, and [F2] preserves their independence. The change-of-variables identity [F10] gives $\mathbb E_{P_j}|Z_i|=\mathbb E_{Q_j}|Z|<\infty$ and $\mathbb E_{P_j}Z_i=\mu_j:=\mathbb E_{Q_j}Z$. Thus [F3] gives $t^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^t Z_i\to\mu_j$ almost surely under $P_j$.

Put $G_t=\prod_{i=1}^t\lambda(X_i)$. By [F6], $G_t$ is a version of the finite-time density, so the algorithm's chosen representative $L_t$ equals $G_t$ $P_0$-almost surely by uniqueness of Radon–Nikodym derivatives. The representative $\lambda$ is finite and strictly positive $Q_0$-almost surely; equivalence of $Q_0,Q_1$ gives the same under $Q_1$. Thus $G_t$ is finite and strictly positive $P_0$-almost surely, and for $A\in\mathcal F_t$, $P_1(A)=\int_A G_t\,dP_0$ implies $P_1(A)=0$ exactly when $P_0(A)=0$. The finite-time restrictions are therefore equivalent, so $L_t=G_t$ also $P_1$-almost surely. Intersecting these probability-one events over countably many $t$ gives one event under each law on which the equalities hold for every $t$. Positivity of $\lambda$ there yields $\log L_t=\sum_{i=1}^tZ_i$.

Under $P_0$, steps 1.2 and 2.1 give $\log L_t/t\to\mu_0<0$, hence $\log L_t\to-\infty$. Since $\log\beta$ is finite, some finite $t$ satisfies $L_t\le\beta$, so the lower boundary has been crossed and the algorithm has $\tau<\infty$.

Under $P_1$, steps 1.2 and 2.1 give $\log L_t/t\to\mu_1>0$, hence $\log L_t\to+\infty$. Since $\log(1/\alpha)$ is finite, some finite $t$ satisfies $L_t\ge1/\alpha$, so the upper boundary has been crossed and $\tau<\infty$. This proves almost-sure termination under both laws, without a claim about $\mathbb E_{P_j}\tau$.

$$\bar X_t:=\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^tX_i,\qquad C_t:=\Theta\cap\left[\bar X_t-\frac{u_\alpha(t\sigma^2)}{t},\,\bar X_t+\frac{u_\alpha(t\sigma^2)}{t}\right],$$
where $u_\alpha$ is from [[def-gaussian-mixture-confidence-sequence-boundary]], and set $C_0:=\Theta$. Then $(C_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence sequence for $\theta$:
$$P_\theta\bigl(\theta\in C_t\text{ for every }t\ge0\bigr)\ge1-\alpha\quad(\theta\in\Theta).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] with $\rho'=1/\tau^2$, $v=0$, and $s=\lambda$. Since $N(0,\tau^2)=N(0,1/\rho')$ by [F1], this gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Y_t}=e^{\lambda^2\tau^2/2}$, finite for every real $\lambda$.

Fix $t$ and $\lambda$. The map $y\mapsto e^{\lambda y}$ is Borel, so for each Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage is Borel; the stated factorization for $Y_t$ therefore gives the same factorization for $e^{\lambda Y_t}$. This variable is integrable by step 1.1, so [F3] yields $\mathbb E[e^{\lambda Y_t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\mathbb E[e^{\lambda Y_t}]$. Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a finite integer
maximum $K\ge1$, prescheduled information fractions
$0<t_1<\cdots<t_K=1$ (where $t_j$ is the fraction of total planned
information available at look $j$), and a nominal level $\alpha\in(0,1)$. An
**alpha-spending function** is a nondecreasing map
$A:[0,1]\to[0,\alpha]$ with $A(0)=0$ and $A(1)=\alpha$.

Under the stipulated simple null law $P_0$, the standardized look vector is
$Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K)\sim N_K(0,\Sigma)$, where
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\sqrt{t_j/t_k}\quad(j\le k),\qquad \Sigma_{jk}=\Sigma_{kj}\quad(j>k).$$
Here $N_K$ is the finite-dimensional multivariate normal law of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], whose projection characterization determines
the law by [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]].
The construction of this covariance matrix as a valid Gaussian covariance is
proved in [[thm-group-sequential-alpha-spending-calibration]]. The standardized
coordinates are correlated; independence of the $Z_j$ is not assumed.

For a **one-sided upper-boundary design**, look $j$ rejects when
$Z_j\ge b_j$. For a **symmetric two-sided design**, look $j$ rejects when
$|Z_j|\ge c_j$. In either case, the procedure stops at its first crossing.
For each $k$, its cumulative type-I probability is the probability under the
stipulated null law of crossing at one of looks $1,\ldots,k$. The design is
exactly calibrated to $A$ when this cumulative probability equals $A(t_k)$
for every $k$. If it is embedded in an experiment with a nonempty alternative
and singleton null hypothesis, this null rejection probability is the test
size in the sense of [[def-test-size-and-power]].

The fractions and joint null law are assumptions of this definition. It does
not derive a Gaussian model from an asymptotic central limit theorem, justify
data-dependent look timing, justify estimated variance, or establish error
control over an unspecified composite null. A two-sided design calibrates its
two-sided crossing events separately; one-sided boundaries are not doubled
to obtain two-sided boundaries.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

**Inputs:** The Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and a canonical design from
[[def-group-sequential-alpha-spending-design]] and a mode, either one-sided
upper-boundary or symmetric two-sided.

**Output:** The look boundaries for the selected mode.

Set $t_0=0$, $R_0=\varnothing$, and process $k=1,\ldots,K$ in order. Let
$R_{k-1}$ be the union of the crossing events already defined at the earlier
looks.

- If $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$, set the boundary at look $k$ to $+\infty$. Its
  crossing event is empty, so $R_k=R_{k-1}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is one-sided, choose the real number
  $b_k$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is symmetric two-sided, choose
  $c_k\ge0$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\}$.

The root-existence theorem
[[thm-group-sequential-alpha-spending-calibration]] proves that every
positive spending increment has a unique finite solution; the algorithm
therefore makes no arbitrary boundary selection. The procedure specifies
exact boundaries under the supplied joint null law. It does not prescribe a
numerical integration package or tolerance.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $1\le i\le j\le K$, define a lower-triangular matrix $L$ by $L_{j1}=\sqrt{t_1/t_j}$ and, for $2\le i\le j$, $L_{ji}=\sqrt{(t_i-t_{i-1})/t_j}$, with $L_{ji}=0$ for $i>j$. For $j\le k$, the $(j,k)$ entry of $LL^T$ is $$\frac{t_1+\sum_{i=2}^{j}(t_i-t_{i-1})}{\sqrt{t_jt_k}}=\sqrt{t_j/t_k}=\Sigma_{jk}.$$ Thus $\Sigma=LL^T$. Its diagonal entries in $L$ are $1$ and $\sqrt{(t_i-t_{i-1})/t_i}>0$ for $i\ge2$, so $L$ is invertible and $v^T\Sigma v=\|L^Tv\|^2>0$ for every nonzero $v$.

For every $k$, the $k$th coordinate has law $N(0,1)$ by the projection clause in [F2]. It has no atoms, and for $x<y$, $$0<P_0(x<Z_k<y)=\int_x^y\phi(u)\,du\le\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$$ Positivity follows from [F5]; the upper bound follows from $0<e^{-u^2/2}\le1$. The same facts bound a two-sided strip by $P_0(c<|Z_k|<d)\le2(d-c)/\sqrt{2\pi}$ when $0\le c<d$.

By [F2] and [F3], the canonical law exists and is represented by $Z=\Sigma^{1/2}Y$ for independent standard-normal coordinates $Y$. Since $\Sigma$ is positive definite by step 1.1, $\Sigma^{1/2}$ is invertible: if $\Sigma^{1/2}v=0$, then $v^T\Sigma v=0$, forcing $v=0$. The inverse image under this linear homeomorphism of any nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^K$ is nonempty and open, hence contains a product of nonempty open intervals. Each interval has positive standard-normal probability by [F4]–[F5], and independence makes the product probability positive. Therefore every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^K$ has positive $P_0$-probability.

For the induction step, fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. Assume that the boundaries through $k-1$ have been constructed with $P_0(R_{k-1})=A(t_{k-1})$; for $k=1$ this is the empty base case $R_0=\varnothing$, $A(t_0)=A(0)=0$. Any finite two-sided boundary already constructed is positive, as established when its root was obtained. Let $S=R_{k-1}^c$. In the one-sided mode, $S$ is the intersection of the open conditions $Z_j<b_j$ for earlier finite boundaries; in the symmetric two-sided mode, it is the intersection of $|Z_j|<c_j$ for earlier finite boundaries. These conditions describe a nonempty open set: choose each constrained coordinate below its upper boundary, or inside its interval $(-c_j,c_j)$, and ignore infinite boundaries. Thus $P_0(S)=1-A(t_{k-1})\ge1-\alpha>0$.

In the one-sided mode set $q(x)=A(t_{k-1})+P_0(S\cap\{Z_k\ge x\})$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. If $x<y$, then $q(x)-q(y)=P_0(S\cap\{x\le Z_k<y\})>0$. Although $S\subseteq\mathbb R^K$, it restricts only coordinates $j<k$, as described in step 3.1. Thus $O_{x,y}:=S\cap\{z\in\mathbb R^K:x<z_k<y\}$ is nonempty and open: choose each earlier coordinate below its finite one-sided boundary (or arbitrarily when its boundary is $+\infty$), choose $z_k\in(x,y)$, and choose the remaining coordinates arbitrarily. By step 2.1, $P_0(O_{x,y})>0$; the only part of $S\cap\{x\le Z_k<y\}$ omitted from $O_{x,y}$ lies on $Z_k=x$, which has probability zero by step 1.2. Also $|q(x)-q(y)|\le(y-x)/\sqrt{2\pi}$ by step 1.2, so $q$ is continuous. Moreover $q(x)\to1$ as $x\to-\infty$ and $q(x)\to A(t_{k-1})$ as $x\to+\infty$, since the omitted lower and upper normal tails tend to zero. For the symmetric two-sided mode set $q(c)=A(t_{k-1})+P_0(S\cap\{|Z_k|\ge c\})$ for $c\ge0$. For $0\le c<d$, $q(c)-q(d)=P_0(S\cap\{c\le|Z_k|<d\})>0$. Here $S$ again restricts only coordinates $j<k$, so $O_{c,d}:=S\cap\{z\in\mathbb R^K:c<|z_k|<d\}$ is nonempty and open: set every earlier coordinate to $0$ (which satisfies every finite earlier symmetric no-crossing condition because its boundary is positive), choose $z_k=(c+d)/2$, and choose the remaining coordinates arbitrarily. Step 2.1 gives $P_0(O_{c,d})>0$. The bound in step 1.2 makes $q$ continuous. Here $q(0)=1$ and $q(c)\to A(t_{k-1})$ as $c\to+\infty$. The tail limits in both modes follow from [F6] applied to increasing lower or central intervals of the standard-normal coordinate.

Since $A$ is nondecreasing, either $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$ or $A(t_{k-1})<A(t_k)\le\alpha<1$. In the flat case, [F9] assigns $+\infty$, whose crossing event is empty, so the previous cumulative probability is unchanged. In the increasing case, the target lies strictly between the endpoint limits of $q$. The limits in step 3.2 give finite endpoints on which the continuous function takes values on opposite sides of $A(t_k)$; [F7] gives a root. Strict decrease in step 3.2 makes that finite root unique. The induction therefore defines every boundary through the finite maximum $K$. In the symmetric two-sided mode $q(0)=1>A(t_k)$, so the root is strictly positive.

The induction step is complete: at an increasing look the selected root gives $P_0(R_k)=A(t_k)$ by [F9]; at a flat look the event union is unchanged and $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$. Induction from $R_0=\varnothing$ proves the equality for every $k$. Stopping at the first crossing makes $R_k$ exactly the event of rejection by look $k$. At $k=K$, $t_K=1$ and $A(1)=\alpha$, so the terminal simple-null rejection probability is $\alpha$. For any embedding with a nonempty alternative and singleton null $\{\theta_0\}$ whose law is $P_0$, the rejection indicator is a measurable test function because $R_K$ is a finite union of Borel threshold events; [F8] then makes its size $\alpha$. AC is used in the supplied Gaussian law and representation [F2] and [F4], not in the finite root selection: each root is unique and there are only finitely many looks.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a finite integer
maximum $K\ge1$, prescheduled information fractions
$0<t_1<\cdots<t_K=1$ (where $t_j$ is the fraction of total planned
information available at look $j$), and a nominal level $\alpha\in(0,1)$. An
**alpha-spending function** is a nondecreasing map
$A:[0,1]\to[0,\alpha]$ with $A(0)=0$ and $A(1)=\alpha$.

Under the stipulated simple null law $P_0$, the standardized look vector is
$Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K)\sim N_K(0,\Sigma)$, where
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\sqrt{t_j/t_k}\quad(j\le k),\qquad \Sigma_{jk}=\Sigma_{kj}\quad(j>k).$$
Here $N_K$ is the finite-dimensional multivariate normal law of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], whose projection characterization determines
the law by [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]].
The construction of this covariance matrix as a valid Gaussian covariance is
proved in [[thm-group-sequential-alpha-spending-calibration]]. The standardized
coordinates are correlated; independence of the $Z_j$ is not assumed.

For a **one-sided upper-boundary design**, look $j$ rejects when
$Z_j\ge b_j$. For a **symmetric two-sided design**, look $j$ rejects when
$|Z_j|\ge c_j$. In either case, the procedure stops at its first crossing.
For each $k$, its cumulative type-I probability is the probability under the
stipulated null law of crossing at one of looks $1,\ldots,k$. The design is
exactly calibrated to $A$ when this cumulative probability equals $A(t_k)$
for every $k$. If it is embedded in an experiment with a nonempty alternative
and singleton null hypothesis, this null rejection probability is the test
size in the sense of [[def-test-size-and-power]].

The fractions and joint null law are assumptions of this definition. It does
not derive a Gaussian model from an asymptotic central limit theorem, justify
data-dependent look timing, justify estimated variance, or establish error
control over an unspecified composite null. A two-sided design calibrates its
two-sided crossing events separately; one-sided boundaries are not doubled
to obtain two-sided boundaries.

**Inputs:** The Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and a canonical design from
[[def-group-sequential-alpha-spending-design]] and a mode, either one-sided
upper-boundary or symmetric two-sided.

**Output:** The look boundaries for the selected mode.

Set $t_0=0$, $R_0=\varnothing$, and process $k=1,\ldots,K$ in order. Let
$R_{k-1}$ be the union of the crossing events already defined at the earlier
looks.

- If $A(t_k)=A(t_{k-1})$, set the boundary at look $k$ to $+\infty$. Its
  crossing event is empty, so $R_k=R_{k-1}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is one-sided, choose the real number
  $b_k$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{Z_k\ge b_k\}$.
- If $A(t_k)>A(t_{k-1})$ and the mode is symmetric two-sided, choose
  $c_k\ge0$ satisfying
  $$P_0(R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\})=A(t_k),$$
  and set $R_k=R_{k-1}\cup\{|Z_k|\ge c_k\}$.

positive spending increment has a unique finite solution; the algorithm
therefore makes no arbitrary boundary selection. The procedure specifies
exact boundaries under the supplied joint null law. It does not prescribe a
numerical integration package or tolerance.

Assume AC and the canonical group-sequential design of

A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC. For nonnegative measurable $X$ (possibly infinite), $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is the unique almost-sure class of nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable $Y$ satisfying $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. If $0\le X_n\uparrow X$ almost surely, then $E[X_n\mid\mathcal G]\uparrow E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Every increasing integrable nonnegative approximation to $X$ gives the same class. For integrable real $V_n\downarrow V$ almost surely with $V_0,V\in L^1$, $E[V_n\mid\mathcal G]\downarrow E[V\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC. Let $P_0$ be one fixed null probability law on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$,
and let $\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F$ be the interim sigma-algebra. Let
$R_0\in\mathcal F$ be the original design's rejection event, and let
$R_1\in\mathcal F$ be the adapted design's event of any eventual rejection,
including early and final decisions. Choose versions
$$A=E_0[\mathbf1_{R_0}\mid\mathcal F_1],\qquad Q=E_0[\mathbf1_{R_1}\mid\mathcal F_1].$$
For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, if $P_0(R_0)\le\alpha$ and $Q\le A$ almost surely,
then $P_0(R_1)\le\alpha$. The original conditional error $A$ is an
almost-sure class; changing its version does not change any rejection
probability.

derivations.claim: For each integer $n\ge1$, define $A_n=2^{-n}\lceil2^nA\rceil$. Its level sets are $\{A_n=0\}=\{A=0\}$ and $\{A_n=k2^{-n}\}=\{(k-1)2^{-n}<A\le k2^{-n}\}$ for $1\le k\le2^n$, so they are in $\mathcal F_1$. The inequality $\lceil2x\rceil\le2\lceil x\rceil$ shows $A_{n+1}\le A_n$, and $0\le A_n-A<2^{-n}$, hence $A_n$ is finite-valued and $A_n\downarrow A$. Write its values as $t_{n,k}=k2^{-n}$, $k=0,\ldots,2^n$, and put $S_{n,k}=\{A_n=t_{n,k}\}$. By [F2], the events $\{p_2\le t_{n,k}\}$ are measurable. Let $Q_n=E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le A_n\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]$. The disjoint partition by $S_{n,k}$, linearity [F5], and taking out the bounded known indicator [F3] give $Q_n=\sum_{k=0}^{2^n}\mathbf1_{S_{n,k}}E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le t_{n,k}\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le\sum_{k=0}^{2^n}t_{n,k}\mathbf1_{S_{n,k}}=A_n$ almost surely. The events $B_n=\{p_2\le A_n\}$ decrease to $B=\{p_2\le A\}$. Their complement indicators are bounded and hence integrable, and increase to $\mathbf1_{B^c}$. Thus [F4] gives $E_0[\mathbf1_{B_n^c}\mid\mathcal F_1]\uparrow E_0[\mathbf1_{B^c}\mid\mathcal F_1]$ almost surely. By linearity and the constant rule [F5], this is equivalent to $Q_n\downarrow Q:=E_0[\mathbf1_B\mid\mathcal F_1]$. Taking limits in step 1.1 and using $A_n\downarrow A$ yields $Q\le A$ almost surely.

Apply [F6] to $R_2=B$: its conditional rejection probability is the $Q$ of step 2.1 and is at most $A$, while the original conditional-error budget has expectation at most $\alpha$. Therefore $P_0(R_2)\le\alpha$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P_0)$ be a probability space, let
$\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F$ be the interim sigma-algebra, let
$N$ be an $\mathcal F_1$-measurable sample size taking values in a nonempty
set $M\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$, and let $p_N$ be the selected stage-2 p-value. For
$m\in M$, put $D_m=\{N=m\}$. Suppose that for every $m\in M$, every fixed
$u\in[0,1]$, and every $H\in\mathcal F_1$,
$$P_0(H\cap D_m\cap\{p_N\le u\})\le uP_0(H\cap D_m).$$
Then for every fixed $u\in[0,1]$,
$$E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_N\le u\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le u\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
Thus conditional validity within each selected-size stratum implies
conditional superuniformity after an interim-measurable finite sample size is
selected, even when the set of allowed sample sizes is countably infinite.

Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[thm-conditional-error-budget-two-stage-adaptation]], let $p_2$ be a
measurable stage-2 p-value with values in $[0,1]$. Suppose that for every
fixed $u\in[0,1]$,
$$E_0[\mathbf1_{\{p_2\le u\}}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le u\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
Then the adapted rejection event $R_2=\{p_2\le A\}$ satisfies
$$E_0[\mathbf1_{R_2}\mid\mathcal F_1]\le A\quad\text{almost surely},$$
and hence $P_0(R_2)\le\alpha$. The conditional p-value inequality is assumed
separately for each fixed $u$; no common exceptional set over all
$u\in[0,1]$ is required.

derivations.claim: Put $\Omega=\{0,1\}^4$ with the uniform law and let $I,B_0,B_2,B_3$ be the independent fair-bit coordinates. Define $p_j=1/2$ when $B_j=0$ and $p_j=1$ when $B_j=1$, for $j\in\{0,2,3\}$. Each $p_j$ is measurable with values in $[0,1]$, and its null CDF is $0$ for $u<1/2$, $1/2$ for $1/2\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$, so each is a valid p-value by [F3]. Let $\mathcal F_1=\sigma(I)$, select $N=2$ on $I=0$ and $N=3$ on $I=1$, and take the original rejection event $R_0=\{p_0\le1/2\}$. Independence and [A1, F4] give its conditional error $A=E_0[\mathbf1_{R_0}\mid\mathcal F_1]=1/2$ almost surely; [F5] makes the resulting event probabilities version-independent. For each $m\in\{2,3\}$ and $H\in\mathcal F_1$, independence of $B_m$ from $I$ gives $P_0(H\cap\{N=m\}\cap\{p_N\le u\})=c(u)P_0(H\cap\{N=m\})$, where $c(u)=0$ for $u<1/2$, $1/2$ for $1/2\le u<1$, and $1$ for $u=1$; in every case $c(u)\le u$. Thus [F1] makes $p_N$ conditionally superuniform. Rejection at $A=1/2$ is exactly the event that the selected bit is zero. Since $P_0(R_0)=P_0(B_0=0)=1/2$, set $\alpha=1/2$ in the overall conclusion of [F2] to obtain $P_0(p_N\le A)\le1/2$; the selected bit is fair, so equality holds and the original budget is attained.

The positive density makes $\Phi$ continuous and strictly increasing. Define the one-sided stage p-values $p_i=1-\Phi(Z_i)$, so $Z_i=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_i)$; for $0<u<1$, $P_0(p_i\le u)=P_0(Z_i\ge\Phi^{-1}(1-u))=u$, and the endpoint inequalities are immediate, so they are valid by [F3]. Fix $c>0$ and set $\alpha=\int_c^\infty\phi(t)\,dt$, with $0<\alpha<1/2$ by positivity and evenness. Under the fixed equal-weight inverse-normal rule, reject when $W=(Z_1+Z_2)/\sqrt2\ge c$. The orthogonal change of variables $w=(z_1+z_2)/\sqrt2$, $v=(z_1-z_2)/\sqrt2$ has absolute Jacobian $1$ and satisfies $z_1^2+z_2^2=w^2+v^2$, so the joint density transforms to $\phi(w)\phi(v)$ and integration over $w\ge c$ gives the fixed-rule null rejection probability $\alpha$.

Choose $N_2=1$ when $Z_1\ge0$ and $N_2=2$ when $Z_1<0$. Without recalibrating $c$, use weights $w(N_2)=(1,0)$ in the first case and $(0,1)$ in the second; each has squared norm one. Since $c>0$, the adapted rejection event is the disjoint union $\{Z_1\ge c\}\cup\{Z_1<0,Z_2\ge c\}$, whose probability by independence is $\alpha+(1/2)\alpha=3\alpha/2>\alpha$. Thus unit-norm weights selected with the stage-2 size do not by themselves preserve the fixed-rule error probability.
